en: The First Volume of the *Huayan jing nei zhangmen deng za kongmu* (Comprehensive Catalogue of the Internal Chapters and Sections of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Taiyi in Zhongnan. Chapter One:
A Comparative Analysis of Ten Gates Regarding the Intent of the Sūtra.
The Heavenly King Praising the Buddha: The First Verse Revealing the Scope of the Teaching;
Chapter One on the Meaning of the One Vehicle and Three Vehicles from the *Lushena* (Vairocana) Section;
the Verse by the Bodhisattva Supreme Sound Establishing the Chapter on Turning the Wheel of Dharma.
The section on "Contemplating the Five Seas" explains the ten knowledges; the section on "Establishing the Five Seas" explains the textual divisions;
within that, the section on "Causes and Conditions for the Pure Land" first establishes the chapter on the Ten Worlds;
and in the section concerning the youth Samantavyūha, the chapter on Cause and Effect is established.
The Second Assembly: Chapter on Names and Titles, Part One: Chapter on the Ritual for Paying Homage to the Buddha, Chapter on the Ten Epithets, Chapter on the Four Modes of Birth.
The Chapter on the Tenfold Pure Land;
the Chapter on Establishing the Four Truths within the Chapter on the Four Truths;
and the Chapter on the Accomplishment of Karma within the Chapter on the Radiance of Awakening.
The Chapter on the Five Aggregates,
appended by the Chapter on the Eighteen Elements,
and further including the Chapter on the Twelve Bases.
The Chapter on Clarifying Difficulties, Part One: Establishing the Section on Consciousness-Only.

The Textual Inquiry Regarding Mañjuśrī’s Questions. The Chapter on Clarifying Entry into the Buddha’s Realm, Number One. Section One: The First Assembly. Section One: A Tenfold Analysis of the Meaning of the Sūtra. Regarding the tenfold analysis of the meaning of this entire sūtra in the first assembly: [The ten gates of the analysis of the meaning of the sūtra in the first assembly. Regarding the meaning of the entire sūtra as analyzed through these ten gates in the first assembly:
At the beginning of this assembly, the phrase "Thus have I heard" first provides a preliminary analysis of the meanings indicated in the subsequent text.
This is categorized into ten gates:
namely, person and dharma; principle and phenomenon; matter and meaning; text and interpretation; practice and realization; cause and fruit.
First, the principal and its attendants are established to clarify the underlying intent.
These are understood as the transformational principal and those who assist in the transformation;
their depth and shallowness, as well as their breadth and narrowness, vary accordingly.
This may be understood by analogy:
humans are themselves Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the distinction between shallow and deep refers to their respective levels of realization.
That is to say, from the three evil realms,
humans, devas, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas—
through the gradual teaching, the sudden teaching, and the perfect teaching— they attain the realization of becoming Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
The degrees of depth differ,
and the same applies to their breadth.
Regarding the depth of the Dharma:
Regarding the stages:
from the initial stage of non-retrogression up to the ultimate ten bhūmis,
one perceives the distinctions among phenomena.
All are entirely different;
their breadth and narrowness are likewise so.
As for the shallowness and depth of their principles:
From the initial worldly knowledge of reality up to the ultimate realization of the *dharmadhātu*,
the various forms of liberation and mastery are all distinct from one another.
The same applies to their breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the depth of the matters involved:
from ordinary worldlings up to the *ekāntika* (those bound to one more birth).
Even unto the realm of the Pure Land of the Dharma Hall of Unimpeded Liberation, where the radiance of the Sun-like Heated Heaven shines, the characteristics of the phenomena differ;
their breadth and narrowness are likewise so.
This explains the shallow and the deep.
The teachings differ in being either secret or manifest,
which results in some giving rise to understanding while others do not.
The same applies to their breadth and narrowness.
As for the shallowness or depth of their practice,
it is like the distinct differences between rabbits, horses, and other such animals.
This causes their karmic actions to differ as well;
the same applies to the breadth and narrowness [of their scope].
As for the depth of their meaning:
The distinctions between the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle differ;
consequently, the meanings they expound vary in depth,
and their scope likewise differs in breadth and narrowness.
Regarding the shallowness and depth of the text:
because the verbal expressions that convey meaning differ— such as being with words or wordless—
the levels of shallowness and depth are not uniform.
The same applies to their breadth and narrowness.
As for the cause being shallow or deep,
it follows from their respective names and numbers.
The first six [factors] have four conditions as their causes;
next, from the present and the projecting [causes] up to the twenty causes and so forth;
finally, they act as mutual causes for one another.
If one distinguishes the depth of the causes according to principle,

they range from the initial objective realm of the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) up to the six aspects of the cause of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), such as the cause of phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta*).
The degrees of depth differ;
the same applies to their breadth and narrowness.
As for the depth of the fruits:
From the initial outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*),
up to the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*) and the retributive maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*),
there are both mundane and supramundane [results].
From the supramundane up to the ultimate state of Buddhahood, they are not the same;
their breadth and narrowness are likewise so.
This concludes the meaning of the ten preceding sections.
The Buddhas, through their skillful means, harmoniously integrate the Dharma-realm with perfect penetration and mastery;
without departing from seeing and hearing,
they realize the subtle Indra-net of Samantabhadra.
Liberation, supernormal powers, and clear insight are then brought to ultimate completion.

Regarding the first verse of the *Tianwang zanfo shuojie choushou xianjiao fenqi yi* (The Meaning of the Exposition of the Limits of the Teaching in the First Verse of the Hymn to the Buddha Spoken by the Heavenly King): based upon the teaching, there are five distinct stages of differentiation.
First, according to the Hīnayāna,
teachings that express names elucidate meanings that possess names;
this pertains to the stage of conceptual differentiation and pervasive imagination.
The teaching of having names elucidates the meaning of having names;
the teaching of having names elucidates the meaning of namelessness.
This is where one should turn the mind.
The meaning within the stage of the initial teaching should be understood as the teaching that names are themselves empty.
The third is the teaching of "having names" which refers to meanings that possess names.
The teaching of having names refers to the meaning of namelessness;
the teaching of namelessness refers to the meaning of namelessness.
This corresponds to the principle that within the stage of matured teaching, existence is established as being identical with the fundamental nature.
This is not what is meant by "existence.
The teaching of the fourfold namelessness reveals the meaning of namelessness;
this meaning properly belongs within the stage of the Sudden Teaching.
This is the teaching of the Samādhi of One Reality.
The teaching of "having names" explains the meaning of having names;
the teaching of "having no names" reveals the meaning of having no names.
This shall be explained in the context of the stage of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) regarding the locus of seeing and hearing:
a teaching that possesses names reveals meanings that possess names;
a teaching that possesses names reveals meanings that are nameless.
The teaching of the nameless reveals the meaning of the nameless;
this is explained from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao),
for the purpose of encompassing inexhaustible meanings.
The scope of the limit refers to the true dharmas known by śrāvakas and ordinary worldly beings;
it encompasses both the textual and doctrinal aspects of the three vehicles, including the Hīnayāna,
as well as the stages of inference and realization within the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya).
The following sutra:
all its words and meanings should be understood by analogy with this.

In the section on the Meaning of the One Vehicle and Three Vehicles within the *Samantabhadra* chapter at the conclusion of the "Cloud Assembly" at the end of the *Vairocana Buddha* chapter, the scripture states:
Those who enter the unsurpassed path should be taught gradually;
it is impossible to exhaust the ground of merit and wisdom.
"Those who are matured in the stage of teaching" refers to the gradual teaching;
"those within the ocean of the nature of vows" refers to the sudden teaching.
This is stated in terms of the limit of the cessation of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
It further says:
"Those who enter the unsurpassed path."
The sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*) and the mature teaching (*shu-jiao*) correspond to the ultimate teaching (*zhong-jiao*) and its underlying meaning.
"The ground of inexhaustible merit and wisdom" refers to the teaching and meaning of the section on Samantabhadra’s practice and realization (*jie-xing*).
"Those within the ocean of the nature of vows" refers to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao);
it is precisely that which begins from the stage of realization (zhengfen) onward.
This is also precisely the practice and vow of Samantabhadra.
The name and characteristics of this vehicle are fully explained within the dialogue;
here, we shall rely on the subsequent scripture.
Regarding the meaning of the five vehicles,
there are three types:
first, humans and devas share one vehicle.
Second, the teachings common to both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas constitute the second category.
Third, the gradual teachings from beginning to end constitute the third category.
Fourth, the sudden teaching stands alone as the first [of its kind].
The first is the Single Vehicle alone,
which collectively constitutes the five vehicles.
As for the second:
Humanity is one; heaven is one;
the śrāvakas are one.
The Pratyekabuddhas constitute one;
the Mahāyāna constitutes another;
and the third is—
The One Heaven, the One Brahma, the One Śrāvaka, the One Pratyekabuddha, and the One Tathāgata—
by uniting these five vehicles,
one achieves the non-discriminative, signless Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
From the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
"If it concerns ordinary beings or those on the vehicle of devas,
the Buddha appears before ordinary beings."
Like those humans and devas,
they lead ordinary persons to cultivate the merits of humans and devas.
Since there are no untainted states (*anāsrava*),
one does not distinguish between the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); rather,
one discusses only mundane meditative concentrations (*laukika-dhyāna-samādhi*).
This constitutes mundane cultivation.
Regarding the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna],
this refers to both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
One immediately reaches the ultimate,
attaining Buddhahood or Arhatship,
proceeding through the twelve stages of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
These are combined with the four fruits and so forth to collectively constitute the twelve abodes (*dvādaśa-vihāra*).
As for these twelve abodes:
First, abiding in one's own śrāvaka lineage;
second, abiding in the skillful means of entering correctly but not yet transcending the gradual stages to attain realization;
third, abiding in the transcendence of the gradual stages to attain realization.
Fourth, the dwelling in the exhaustion of outflows through the superior noble ethical discipline that has attained the flavor of the four kinds of unshakable confidence;
fifth, the dwelling born from the training in higher ethics and higher mind;
sixth, seventh, and eighth, the dwellings in the training in higher wisdom through the attainment of knowledge of the true realities.
Ninth, dwelling in the signless samādhi through the observation of arising;
tenth, dwelling in the ultimate signlessness;
eleventh, dwelling in the liberation from the points of training.
The twelfth is the stage of the Arhat who abides in all modes;
the Bodhisattva who proceeds directly possesses the ten stages within a single person.
He further explains that one attains Buddhahood only after the stages of seeing and cultivation,
and he sets forth the twelve abodes of the Mahāyāna.
As for these twelve abodes:
1. Abiding in the single lineage;
2. Abiding in the stage of practice through understanding;
3. Abiding in the pure mind.
4. The dwelling of higher ethical discipline;
5. The dwelling of higher mind;
6. The dwelling of higher wisdom.
Seventh is the dwelling of wisdom associated with the seven truths.
Eighth is the dwelling of wisdom associated with dependent origination.
Ninth is the signless dwelling that involves effort and development.
10. The dwelling of signlessness without activity or development;
11. The dwelling of unimpeded wisdom;
12. The supreme bodhisattva dwelling.
If one is at the stage of mature instruction,
it is not the same as the previous meaning;
this refers to the period prior to the first bhūmi.
There is death by fragmentation;
those who have previously attained the untainted (anāsrava) also possess death by transformation (pariṇāmikī-maraṇa).
From the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi,
there is death through transformation (parināma-maraṇa).
Only after the fulfillment of the ten stages does one finally attain Buddhahood;
this is according to the Sudden Teaching.
That is to say, all stages of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are ineffable,
because they are without marks (*animitta*).
This is explained according to the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles.
If one relies on the perfectly comprehensive doctrine of the One Vehicle,
the general and specific aspects are mutually established through the mastery of its meaning.
Therefore, there are no distinctions such as before or after, beginning or end, shallow or deep,
near or far; rather, once one has attained non-retrogression,
one immediately realizes that Dharma of Samantabhadra.
Judging by the teachings concerning the stage of maturity,
this refers to the period from the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā-citta) onward; that is its position.
Within that stage of Samantabhadra,
regarding those dharmas of understanding and practice as well as the meanings attained therein,
there is only the excellence of one's own portion and further progress.
These two meanings are distinct.
His body resides in the station of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) of the Pure White Jewel Net;
such is the sphere of his ten eyes, ten ears, and so forth.
If one defines it according to the limits of the stage of practice through understanding,
one has not yet attained the "stainless samādhi" (vimala-samādhi).
As for this stainless samādhi:
Before receiving his office,
he is fixed in a state where his body dwells in a realm equal to or above that of the world-systems,
yet he remains within the stage of the "all-seeing" physical eye.
One perceives the worlds of the ten directions.
If one realizes the stage of Samantabhadra,
one abides within the ten stages of the sixfold skillful means.
Why is this? Because one relies upon the ten stages to realize the meaning and assemble with the universal Dharma.
If one attains that body which is the basis for the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, [one realizes it].
They shall also attain rebirth among the devas in Tuṣita Heaven, taking on the bodies of sons of gods;
having emerged from the three evil realms,
they are born within that celestial realm.
One attains a body free from obstacles and accomplishes the dharmas of Samantabhadra’s understanding and practice,
just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* describes regarding the female dragon.
The meaning should be that they retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) precisely in order to bring about those bodies born together with others. Why is this?
Because these individuals all possess various kinds of roots of goodness from the past.
Nor is it identical to this body of transformation.
Why? Because the Lotus Sūtra cites that [attainment] as proof of the superiority of its teaching—that rare and supreme practice is swiftly accomplished.
If it were a mere transformation,
it would not be extraordinary;
however, if we discuss it in terms of the extent to which delusions are extinguished:
According to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra," one obstacle encompasses all obstacles;
according to the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics," it explains the limits for severing delusions.
When one is severed, all are severed.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"There are five hundred afflictions each within and without."
Furthermore, the eighty-four thousand afflictions are universally extinguished without exception;
thus it is known.
Why is this? Because it was spoken in contrast to the limits of birth and death.
Furthermore, at the time when he held the rank of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) with a pure white jewel-net.
There is a crystal mirror of Dīpaṃkara whose radiance illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields;
by this one may verify it.
You should know that the rank of the Universal Monarch Śuddhavarṇaratnajāla possesses no small measure of merit.
If they arise for practical benefit,
they immediately cause immeasurable sentient beings to resolve upon non-retrogressive bodhicitta and to aspire toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, while on the tenth stage, the stage of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
one has only attained a small portion of the *vimala-samādhi* (stainless samādhi).
As for the remaining characteristics of the stages, their virtues, functions, and spheres of experience:
Furthermore, the specific details regarding the vision of the Buddha are fully contained within the scriptural texts.
Moreover, as for the meaning of the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna):
There are two types of classification:
first, the direct vehicle;
second, the provisional vehicle.
The True Vehicle is as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, as previously distinguished regarding the vehicle of skillful means (*upāyayāna*),
there are ten such distinctions.
The Three Jewels are distinguished as follows:
the Buddha Jewel is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna),
while the Sangha consists of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna).
Why is this? Because the Buddha is eternally inexhaustible,
whereas the Dharma and the Sangha are not fixed.
Second, distinguishing according to the four truths:
the truth of cessation is the One Vehicle;
the other three truths are the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Because cessation is equally inexhaustible,
whereas the [other] three truths are not fixed.
Third, the distinction according to the two truths:
the ultimate truth is the One Vehicle;
the conventional truth is the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Because the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) is equally inexhaustible.
In conventional truth, it is not fixed.
This is the analysis of the four pairs of faults.
One who is without fear—
That which is the One Vehicle is precisely this;
that which possesses fear is the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Because, as in the case of the Tathāgatagarbha and so forth,
there is no fault when [the teaching] is based upon them.
Because they are likewise inexhaustible:
the six consciousnesses, the mind,
and the knowledge of phenomena— these seven factors.
Moment by moment they do not abide;
they do not plant the seeds of manifold sufferings,
nor do they attain weariness with suffering or seek to attain nirvāṇa.
Because it is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
and because its conditions are not autonomous,
it is analyzed in five pairs with respect to persons and wisdom.
There are three kinds of persons who accomplish three kinds of knowledge.
As for these three kinds of knowledge:
First, suppose a son or daughter of good family has accomplished profound knowledge of the Dharma and is considered as a single person.
Second, if there is a man or woman who has accomplished the conforming knowledge of phenomena (anuloma-dharma-jñāna), they serve as the second person.
Third, if there is a man or woman...
Not understanding these profound dharmas for myself,
I defer to the World-Honored One, [saying]:
"This is not within my sphere."
This is known only by the Buddha.
This is the foremost among the three types of persons;
it is the wisdom of the One Vehicle.
The latter two persons possess the wisdom of the three vehicles. Why is this?
The first wisdom mentioned above is realized wisdom;
because this realized wisdom is identical with the inexhaustible,
the latter two wisdoms [are also so].
Because it has not yet realized the true Dharma,
it is indeterminate;
this is stated according to the Śrīmālā-sūtra.
The six pairs of phenomena that are understood as illusory yet accord with reality and are non-conceptual;
explaining the meaning according to the text—
these are the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Knowing that all is empty and in accord with non-discrimination is the Single Vehicle Dharma. Why is this so?
It accords with non-discrimination,
for it is identical with the inexhaustible.
Those who grasp according to the literal text...
This is not fixed;
it is explained according to the meaning of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as a sevenfold classification of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Lesser Vehicle.
The One Vehicle is indeed the One Vehicle;
the Three Vehicles and so forth are indeed the Three Vehicles. Why is this?
The One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is inexhaustible;
the Three Vehicles and so forth are indeterminate.
This constitutes the eighth pair, distinguishing between the Great Vehicle, the Middle Vehicle, and the Small Vehicle.
The Mahāyāna is itself the One Vehicle.
Why is this? Because the Mahāyāna is supreme and preeminent.
Because it is inexhaustible;
as for the Middle Vehicle and the Lesser Vehicle,
their meanings are not fixed.
As the sutra states, because the three refuges are unified as one,
there are nine categories distinguished according to the mundane, the supramundane, and the ultra-supramundane;
[the ninth being] the ultra-supramundane.
This is the One Vehicle;
the others are the Three Vehicles. Why is this so?
Because the supramundane and the supreme supramundane are equal and inexhaustible,
whereas the other two are not fixed.
This is as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding those who separately requested vehicles outside the enclosure on the open ground.
This refers precisely to that matter.
It is analyzed through ten sets of analogies,
such as the great jewel in the king’s topknot and the great king himself, and so forth.
This is precisely the jewel of the One Vehicle;
it is tied within the garments of you and those such as the impoverished sons.
This is precisely the Three Vehicles. Why is this?
Because the King of Topknot Jewels is extremely profound and secret.
The others are indeterminate.
This is according to the teachings of the Lotus Sūtra.
Thus concludes what has been analyzed above.
In the *Bandhuparivarta-sūtra*,
it is intended to reveal the complete, unobstructed,
and inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teachings and meanings.
Within the context of skillful means,
he reveals the name of the One Vehicle so that those who enter may easily attain understanding.
It is said as follows:
if one proceeds toward the dharma-gates by relying on expedient means,
there are two meanings.
This is explained generally as the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
First, it is established by relying on the teaching of the ultimate One Vehicle. Why is this so?
Because it flows from the One Vehicle,
and because it is designated by the teachings of the One Vehicle;
secondly, [it is distinguished] from that ultimate, perfectly complete One Vehicle.
The One Vehicle is taught as a skillful means;
it does not, however, signify the ultimate meaning of perfect penetration and sovereign mastery.
Other meanings may be understood by analogy.
The aforementioned dharma-gate subsumes all lower teachings and directly belongs to the meaning of the fundamental teaching of the upper division.
Gradually following its ultimate meaning,
it penetrates the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles,
and the Lesser Vehicle. Why is this?
It is designated by the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
as well as the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) of the Three Vehicles;

it encompasses the True Suchness of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇatathatā*)— wherein stillness and illumination are one, and illumination is stillness— as well as the gates of the Initial Teaching (Chujiao).
The teaching on the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which regards defilement and purity as being empty and deluded regarding phenomena,
differs in its tenets from those concerning the real dharmas, such as the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The principles are each distinct.

Regarding the chapter on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma established at the beginning of the verses by the Bodhisattva Sarvadharmavaśavartin: as for "turning the wheel of Dharma," it is as follows.
There are two kinds: first, the transformation into the Single Vehicle;
second, the transformation into the Three Vehicles, specifically the Lesser Vehicle.
Regarding the transformation of the One Vehicle:
there are ten practices within the Single Truth,
as explained in the sutra below.
First, they are fully endowed with the four kinds of fearlessness;
second, they produce the pure and wondrous sounds of the four types of analytical eloquence;
third, they clearly understand the four noble truths.
Fourth, they accord with the Buddhas' unimpeded Dharma-gates.
Fifth, their pure and equanimous minds are able to universally encompass all sentient beings.
Sixth, what he has taught is not in vain;
he is certain to deliver sentient beings from the limits of suffering.
Seventh, he is sustained by the great compassion of his past lives.
Eighth, the sound of the wheel of the sublime Dharma fills the Dharma-realm;
there are no sentient beings who do not hear and know it.
Ninth, for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one constantly preaches the True Dharma.
Without ever ceasing for even a moment,
the ten faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the liberations, and the various dhyānas and samādhis continue in uninterrupted succession.
The remaining three truths are to be understood in the same manner. Furthermore,
when the Dharma flows and enters the minds of sentient beings,
there are ten further causes for the speaker.
What are these ten? They are:
first, by virtue of past vows;
second, being sustained by great compassion.
Because he does not abandon sentient beings,
his wisdom is sovereign,
as he preaches the Dharma to them according to their respective needs.
Because they never miss the proper time;
because they accord with the capacity of those vessels without increase or decrease;
and because they possess the definitive knowledge that discerns the three periods of time.
Because their physical conduct is most excellent;
because their verbal conduct is never false;
and because their wisdom fully awakens to all sounds and voices.
The underlying principle applies equally:
the sentient beings who are the recipients must possess four conditions.
The meaning of this can be understood.
Regarding those who turn the wheel of Dharma within the Three Vehicles— the Small Vehicle and the others—
it is within the scope of a single truth.
It has three turnings,
which constitute twelve aspects;
the other three [turnings] are likewise the same.
This constitutes forty-eight lines,
as explained in the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding the "turning of the wheel of Dharma":
The teaching of the meaning of the Four Noble Truths through three turnings and twelve aspects:
"This is the truth of suffering;
this is the origin of suffering."
"This is the cessation of suffering;
this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—
this is called the one turning with four aspects.
This is the truth of suffering, which should be known;
this is the origin of suffering, which should be abandoned;
this is the cessation of suffering, which should be realized.
"This suffering should be understood; this origin should be abandoned; this cessation should be realized; this path leading to cessation should be cultivated.
This is called the second turning of the four aspects.
Having known that "this is suffering," [one proceeds].
Having abandoned this accumulation of suffering,
having realized this cessation of suffering,
and having cultivated this path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This is called the third turning of the four characteristics.
As for these four characteristics:
within the Four Noble Truths, there arises the eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening.
It is also called "practice.
This refers to the section from the beginning of the *Triyāna-paripācana-śāstra* (The Maturational Teaching of the Three Vehicles) onwards.
The teaching that names are identical and not distinct is called the "Non-maturing" (Avipāka) teaching;
its ultimate meaning is identical to the meaning of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao),
wherein the name "Transformation" (Parāvṛtti) is bestowed solely upon True Suchness (Tathatā).
It is not that what can be transformed is called "transformation.
The aforementioned dharma-gate subsumes all the teachings that follow.
The sudden [teaching] belongs to its primary essence,
dividing the fundamental meaning of the teaching;
the gradual [teaching] follows its secondary meaning.
It encompasses the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Lesser Vehicle. Why is this?
Because it is that which is designated by the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Furthermore, there are the final teachings of the Three Vehicles,
wherein quiescent illumination and illuminating quiescence are the single characteristic of True Suchness, along with the initial teaching gate,
which holds that defilement and purity are immediately empty for those of dull faculties.
Regarding the teaching on the Truth of Suffering in the Hīnayāna,
the doctrines concerning the real dharmas— such as the conditioned and the unconditioned— differ;
their principles and meanings are each distinct.
The Chapter on the Five Oceans Established at the Beginning of the Text Explaining the Ten Knowledges through the Contemplation of the Five Oceans. Regarding the five oceans:
first, the ocean of all world-systems.
Second, the ocean of all sentient beings;
third, the ocean of the realms of nature and karma;
fourth, the ocean of the desires, inclinations, and faculties of all sentient beings.
The five oceans of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Contemplating those five oceans,
one explains the ten knowledges.
First, the wisdom of the purity of the formation and destruction of all oceans of worlds;
second, the wisdom of the arising of all inconceivable realms of sentient beings;
third, the wisdom that observes the dharma-realm.
Fourth, the wisdom of the sovereign mastery of all Tathāgatas;

2. Second Assembly: Chapter on the Names of the Tathāgatas, Part One: Chapter on the Ritual for Paying Homage to the Buddha. Regarding the ritual for paying homage to the Buddha, there are three types.

Regarding these three methods of salutation,

Second is "the similar rite."
Although the physical form is correct,

Third is the ritual that accords with reality.
Its ritual forms accord with proper decorum and correspond with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Alternatively, it may correspond with the true nature,
namely the nature of suchness (tathatā);
this is called "homage in accordance with reality."
The ritual propriety of verbal karma may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Sixth is the prostration of dedication toward enlightenment.

Chapter on the Four Modes of Birth According to the Provisional Path of Enlightenment of the Tathāgata. Regarding the four modes of birth:
they are birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
The four modes of birth pertain to the three realms;
the Buddha is identical to the womb-born;
in the Pure Land, there are two modes of birth.
This refers to moisture-born and transformation-born beings.
Why is this? Because the sense faculties of those born by transformation are instantaneously complete.
Since there are those in the Pure Land lotus flowers who attain birth gradually,
we know that moisture-born beings exist.
This refers to Amitābha Buddha.
They have parents;
by this standard, the Buddha would likewise be of womb-birth (jarāyu-ja).
However, because there is nothing to which he resembles, he is not of womb-birth.
Within the three realms and six paths of existence,
among humans there are four modes of birth,
and among animals there are likewise four.
Among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there is no fixed rule:
if they are "proper" ghosts (*samyak-preta*), they are exclusively of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*);
if they are "borderline" ghosts (*prānta-preta*), they may belong to all four modes of birth.
The hells and the heavens consist solely of beings born by transformation; therefore,
the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
The four modes of birth encompass the six destinies,
but the six destinies do not encompass the modes of birth,
because the six destinies include all four modes of birth.
The four modes of birth encompass the six destinies;

The Chapter on the Ten Kinds of Pure Lands: According to the meaning of the Hīnayāna, there are no distinct pure lands;

First, the transformation pure land (*nirmāṇa-śuddhakṣetra*).
This refers to the manifestation of all pure lands in every direction.
Second is the purity of the land itself,
meaning that the pure lands in all directions are composed of various precious jewels.
Third is the Pure Land of True Reward (vipākaviśuddha-kṣetra).
This refers to that which is accomplished through various principles and practices;
it takes the three gates of emptiness as its entryway.
The various perfections and so forth serve as the paths for entering and exiting;
the four dharmas are the pure land of nature,
namely, suchness (tathatā).
This means that all dharmas are established based upon the foundation of non-abiding.
There are ten points by which the Pure Land of the One Vehicle is established as its standard.
For this sake, throughout all the four continents of this Sahā world-system,
they teach and transform all beings;
first, there are those with various kinds of bodies.
Second, there are various names;
third, there are various locations;
fourth, there are various forms and colors.
7) There are various lengths [of bodies].
8) There are various lifespans.
9) There are various attainments and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Seventh, there are various faculties;
eighth, there are various places of birth;
ninth, there are various karmas.
There are ten kinds of various retributions;
thus, as these are diverse and different,
the perceptions of sentient beings also vary accordingly.
Question: If one wishes to clarify the pure land, why does one instead distinguish the differing capacities of sentient beings?
Answer: The Buddha-land is inherently harmonious and integrated.
It is equal to the dharma-realm;
there is nothing distinct that can be distinguished from it. Why is this?
Because this Buddha-land is coextensive with the dharma-realm,
if one wishes to distinguish its boundaries, they are determined by the differences in the rising and sinking,
and the clarity or turbidity of the water of meditative concentration, which correspond to the increase or decrease in the mental karma and conduct of sentient beings.
The manifestation of the Buddha-land is likewise differentiated.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised the profound uniqueness of that land,
using the appearance of the sentient beings therein as a metaphor for the characteristics of the land itself.
Question: Regarding the One Vehicle Pure Land, what are the distinctions between the Great and Small Vehicles, and between the defiled and the pure?
How can one know the boundaries of their similarities and differences?
Answer: As for the Pure Land of the One Vehicle:
The one is precisely the many;
the many are precisely the one.
This is explained in detail as presented in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
If you wish to know its dimensions,
you may ascertain them by comparing it to those ten Buddhas;

"How is it known that the ālayavijñāna exists?"
If this consciousness did not exist,
then the appropriation [of the body], the initial clarity of seeds, the experience of bodily sensation, the attainment of mindless meditative absorption,
and the process of death would all be irrational.
The explanation of this verse is as stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*:
by means of eight aspects.
It is established that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists;
for if one were apart from the ālayavijñāna,
the appropriation of the basis would be impossible.
Because an initial arising cannot be apprehended;
because a manifest arising cannot be apprehended;
and because the essential nature of a seed cannot be apprehended.
Because the essential nature of karmic activity cannot be apprehended;
because the essential nature of bodily sensation cannot be apprehended;
and because dwelling in the mindless meditative absorption cannot be apprehended.
Because the consciousness at the moment of death cannot be apprehended.
First, why is the appropriation of the basis (āśrayopādāna) unapprehendable?
It is due to five reasons.
That is to say, the ālayavijñāna acts as the causal condition of prior action to bring about the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) such as the visual consciousness;
it acts as the present objective condition to trigger them, just as the sense organs and their objects are described.
"By the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is called the first cause.
Furthermore, the presence of wholesome and unwholesome states within the six groups of consciousness constitutes the second cause.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the six groups of consciousness to be comprised within a single category of the nature of maturation and neutrality;
this is the third reason.
Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness each function based on their respective supports.
Whenever a particular consciousness arises in dependence upon its support,
that consciousness should then grasp and maintain that very support.
It is not logical that the remainder is non-appropriated; even if one were to grant that it is appropriated,
[it would still be untenable].
This is also illogical,
because it would be separate from consciousness;
this is the fourth reason.
Furthermore, the basis [of consciousness] would incur the fault of being repeatedly appropriated. Why is this?
Because of that visual consciousness.
At one time it evolves, and at another time it does not evolve;
the same applies to the other consciousnesses.
This is the fifth reason.
Second, why is it that the initial arising [of consciousness] cannot be apprehended?
This refers to the following objection:
"If there were an ālayavijñāna..."
It would follow that two consciousnesses arise simultaneously in a single sentient being.
You should be told:
"You are falsely conceiving an error where there is no error."
It is possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously.
Why is this? It is because, for example, a single person may simultaneously desire to see, and so on, up to desiring to cognize.
It is not reasonable for any single consciousness to arise first. Why is that?
At that time, there is no distinction in the mental attention (*manasikāra*),
and the faculties and their objects appear without impairment.
For what cause and condition do the consciousnesses not arise simultaneously?
Third, why is it that clear manifestation cannot be established?
It is because if one dogmatically maintains that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously,
[then] they could not share a single object while functioning together with the visual and other sensory consciousnesses.
The clearly discerning mental consciousness (manovijñāna) should be unobtainable. Why is this so?
When one recollects an object previously experienced,
at that time the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises without clarity;
such a lack of clarity is not found in the mental consciousness that arises with respect to a present object.
Therefore, one should believe that the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously;
otherwise, one must admit that the sixth mental consciousness lacks the nature of clarity.
Fourth, why is it that the essential nature of the seeds cannot be apprehended?
This refers to the fact that each of the six groups of evolving consciousnesses is distinct from the others. Why is this so?
Because these six evolving consciousnesses...
From the wholesome, the unwholesome nature arises immediately thereafter;
from the unwholesome, the wholesome nature arises again immediately thereafter;
and from both of these, the indeterminate nature arises immediately thereafter.
From the lower realm, one is born directly into the middle realm;
from the middle realm, one is born directly into the sublime realm;
and from the sublime realm, one is born directly even down to the lower realm.
The untainted arises immediately after the tainted;
the tainted arises immediately after the untainted;
and the supramundane arises immediately after the mundane.
It is not logically tenable that a supramundane state arises immediately after a mundane one,
with such a [mundane] consciousness serving as the substantial seed.
Furthermore, the mental continuum is interrupted for long periods,
yet it continues to flow without ceasing for a long time;
therefore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are able to maintain the seeds.
This is not logical.
Fifth, why is it that the functional activity [of consciousness] cannot be found?
It is because if the various consciousnesses did not arise simultaneously, their functional activities could not proceed together.
This is not logical.
Why is that? Briefly stated, there are four types of karmic activity of consciousness.
That is to say: it discerns the external vessel-world,
it discerns the basis [of existence],
and it is capable of discerning a self.
The discernment of objects:
these four kinds of discerning activities of consciousness manifest simultaneously at every single moment.
It cannot be that such diverse functional activities exist within a single consciousness in a single moment; therefore,
there must necessarily be the simultaneous arising of multiple consciousnesses.
Sixth: Why is it that the essential nature of the body-feeling cannot be apprehended?
It is, for example, as if there were a person who reflects in accordance with reality.
Either through improper reflection,
or through non-reflection,
or again through investigation.
Whether the mind is in meditative concentration or not in meditative concentration,
various and manifold bodily sensations arise.
If the ālayavijñāna did not exist,
such bodily sensations would be impossible to obtain.
Since it is actually perceived [in experience],
the ālayavijñāna must certainly exist.
(7) Why is it that it cannot be perceived in the mindless attainments?
As the Blessed One has said:
"One should know that those who enter the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation [are as follows]."
At that time, consciousness does not depart from the body.
If the ālayavijñāna did not exist,
then at that time consciousness would have to depart from the body.
If consciousness were to depart from the body,
one would immediately lose life;
it does not mean that it remains fixed in its location.
8. Why is it that the consciousness at the time of death cannot be apprehended?
It is because, at the moment of passing away, consciousness gradually abandons and departs from [the body].
Within the constituent parts of the body that serve as the basis,
a sensation of cold arises,
either from above or from below.
It is not that case; for the mental consciousness does not sometimes fail to arise.
Thus it is known.
Only the ālayavijñāna is able to maintain the body,
conforming to each part of the body.
If this consciousness were abandoned,
the sensation of cold could be perceived,
yet the body would have no tactile awareness.
The mental consciousness is not so.
Therefore, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist,
the consciousness at the moment of death could not possibly be found.
Question: As stated in the previous treatise,
"mind" refers to the ālayavijñāna, which contains all seeds and is permeated by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*).
It is also called the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and also called the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*),
because it is able to accumulate all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā):
this refers to the fact that through the manifestation of the aggregates and so forth, all those seeds are brought to increase. Regarding "the consciousness of all seeds":
[it is that which contains] all seeds.
It is called the *ālayavijñāna* because it is that which has accumulated the seeds of all phenomena,
such as the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because it is able to contain and store the seeds of all phenomena,
and because sentient beings grasp it as a self.
As for the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness):
Because it is produced by prior karma,
the ādāna-vijñāna (appropriating consciousness) is that which causes the continuity of birth to arise repeatedly.
It is so called because it maintains the faculties and so forth,
preventing them from being impaired.
Furthermore, as for the term "mind":
Because it is able to accumulate the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena;
according to this textual characteristic,
[it refers to] the *ālayavijñāna*.
It exists within the very midst of phenomena.
How is it known that this is the Tathāgatagarbha?
Answer: Because the Tathāgatagarbha is undefiled yet appears defiled.
Because these phenomenal characteristics do not exist apart from the reality itself,
it is the Tathāgatagarbha; thus,
the treatise says:
Apart from consciousness, there is no other phenomenon whatsoever.
Based on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the ālayavijñāna is established through eight meanings.
First, based on the meaning of the three characteristics,
one knows that the fundamental consciousness exists.
Second, based on the meaning of perfuming, the existence of the fundamental consciousness is established.
Third, based on the principle that they mutually serve as cause and effect,
the existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is established.
Fourth, based on the principle of being neither identical nor different.
The existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is established by way of the fivefold analysis of the distinction and non-distinction between cause and effect. Thus,
the existence of the fundamental consciousness is established.
Sixth, based on the meaning of dependent origination,
the existence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is established.
Seventh, based on the meaning of whether those causes and conditions are complete or incomplete.
The establishment of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) has its basis;
the eight supports are harmonized and brought back to the correct [teaching],
thereby establishing the fundamental consciousness.
Initially, the ālayavijñāna is established by means of its three characteristics.
These three characteristics are:
first, the characteristic of cause.
This encompasses all causes,
yet it takes their mutual causality as the starting point. Why is this?
Because they serve as mutual causes and are subtle, corresponding to consciousness;
these two aspects of the fruit encompass all fruits.
It still begins with the mutual relationship of cause and effect.
The three self-characteristics are precisely the characteristic of maturation (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*) within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) encompasses all phenomena;
this is how it is known.
Based on the seeds of all phenomena,
maturation arises;
it is not restricted solely to the retribution of afflictions and karma.
The habitual tendencies of names and words and so forth are known through their conformity with all associated [mental states].
Question: If this is so, then...
Since both the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*) are equally susceptible to being perfumed (*vāsya*),
for what reason is it said that only the ripening fruit-retribution (*vipāka-phala*) is perfumed?
Answer: Since the present discussion on perfuming (vāsanā) aims to clarify its seeds—
that is, the seed-consciousness—
and because this [consciousness] is already established as that very seed, it is not explained here in contrast to it.
The ripening consciousness is characterized by a neutral (avyākṛta) aspect and is concordant with the perfuming.
Therefore, within the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
its meaning as "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) is analyzed;
now, in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty:
This clarifies the intended meaning of the three characteristics of the ālayavijñāna,
demonstrating that the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is the substance of both cause and effect.
Second, regarding the establishment of the fundamental consciousness through perfuming (vāsanā):
First, it clarifies that the meaning of the formation of perfuming (vāsanā) exists within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), whereas it does not exist in other dharmas.
Second, it clarifies the meaning of their mutual functioning as cause and effect.
Third, it establishes the existence of the fundamental consciousness.
It clarifies that within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) there exists the principle of mutual causality,
whereas this does not apply to other phenomena.
If that is so, for what reason [is it said] regarding bundles of reeds and the like?
It is possible for dharmas to function as causes and effects for one another.
Answer: Among other dharmas, they do indeed function as causes and effects for one another.
This is precisely the gateway for turning toward principle;
it is a provisional designation of cause and effect,
not the ultimate reality.
Fourth, regarding the establishment of the existence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) by way of neither identity nor difference: if,
within the fundamental consciousness, the various phenomena (dharmas) can exist as neither identical nor different [from it].
It cannot be established apart from consciousness.
If one speaks of being neither identical nor different while apart from the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna),
this is merely a figurative designation.
Fifth, regarding the establishment of the existence of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) based on whether cause and effect are distinct or non-distinct:
if there is a fundamental consciousness,
then cause and effect are established as being both distinct and non-distinct.
Apart from consciousness, they do not exist. Why?
Because causes, effects, and seeds cannot be established apart from consciousness.
Sixth, regarding the establishment of the existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) through the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
there are ten sections.
The first concerns the three types of dependent origination.
It establishes that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and reveals its essence, characteristics, and function.
That is to say, dependent origination by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the essence.
Because consciousness is the universal cause for that which arises through conditions,
the two— the pleasant and the unpleasant arising from conditions—
are its characteristics.
Third is the dependent origination of enjoyment,
which is precisely "usage.
Second, delusion is cited to reveal the correct [state].
It is established that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*),
as stated in the treatise:
"To illustrate the delusion of the six teachers regarding the horse."
This is precisely that matter.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it cites the six attachments and so forth as being deluded regarding the Buddha-nature.
One should know that these six attachments are now deluded regarding dependent origination.
Dependent origination is itself Buddha-nature. Why is this?
Because the substance of Buddha-nature possesses various flavors according to the place where it flows.
The remaining meanings may be understood.
Regarding the distinction between the determinate and the indeterminate within the "only consciousness" (vijñaptimātra):
the internal seeds, namely the ālayavijñāna, are exclusively indeterminate.
Alternatively, there are two [categories]: those that are virtuous or non-virtuous by nature, and those that are defiled or pure;
other phenomena do not exist [as such], because apart from consciousness, they are merely conceptual constructions whose very essence is empty.
Fourth, distinguishing between the provisional and the real:
the ālayavijñāna is real;
all other dharmas are provisional.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are nothing but consciousness;
thus, the internal seeds are truly real.
Why is this? Because all phenomena have consciousness as their basis.
Fifth, regarding the six meanings established in relation to the internal:
It perishes moment by moment;
it is accompanied and followed [by its conditions] until the limit of purification, where one definitively contemplates causes and conditions.
Just as drawing forth and manifesting one's own fruit must necessarily possess six factors,
this is the meaning of being a correct cause.
If it were deficient,
it would not be the true teaching;
[it would be the view of] non-Buddhists or śrāvakas.
Such a dharma does not exist.
If external seeds were [the cause], it would be a mere conventional designation.
The rest is explained as in the dialogue.
Sixth, regarding the distinction between those [dharmas] that are perfumed to become seeds and those that are not:
the ālayavijñāna is necessarily perfumed to become seeds;
if other dharmas serve as seeds, they are not perfumed to become them.
Because it is not formed through perfuming, it is not a real seed.
Question: If this is so, then seeds such as rice and barley are not formed through perfuming.
It should not have the meaning of a seed.
Answer: External grains, wheat, and so forth, arise from the perfuming and transformation of the ālayavijñāna.
Grains, wheat, and so forth are conventionally designated as "seeds.
If they were definitively seeds, one would sow grains,
wheat, and so forth [as seeds].
They must necessarily be attained simultaneously;
since they are not accomplished simultaneously, one should know that [this is so].
Karma is the primary seed;
therefore, grains such as rice and barley are merely secondary causes.
This meaning is beyond doubt.
Therefore, the treatise cites the internal as the basis for the external to prove that there is perfuming within;
such is the meaning of perfuming (vāsanā).
The ālayavijñāna possesses four qualities and is thus capable of receiving perfuming.
The first is "stability," meaning it is stable because its principle is real.
All other phenomena apart from consciousness depend upon consciousness and lack autonomy;
they are all entirely insubstantial.
Question: If all phenomena lack solidity, for what reason is the *kṛsara* seed cited as being solid?
Answer: The *kṛsara* seed resembles solidity, yet it is not truly solid.
Why is this? Because it soon disperses and disintegrates;
the ālayavijñāna is not like that.
The karmic fruit is likewise not firm;
because it is established in dependence upon conditions,
it lacks independence.
How could this be firm?
This is logically untenable;
it contradicts the two meanings of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Only then can it receive perfuming.
Why is this? That which is "unspecified" (avyākṛta) has the meaning of being non-conceptual (nirvikalpa).
This dharma exists only within the Tathāgatagarbha. If that is so,
for what reason is its retribution indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
Answer: This is because the wisdom of the śrāvakas is shallow;
to lead them toward the proximate stage, it is taught that the retribution-consciousness receives perfuming.
Retribution has neither essence nor function;
since consciousness constitutes its essence,
it is said that retribution lacks ultimate reality and is indeterminate in nature.
The principle is thus.
Regarding the three factors capable of being perfumed:
only the Tathāgatagarbha does not maintain its own nature.
Because it arises in accordance with the conditions of all phenomena to manifest as an object-like appearance,
it is susceptible to perfuming;
other dharmas are not so.
Since it is bound by conditions,
how could it further undergo the perfuming of various dharmas?
For this reason, other dharmas cannot serve as the perfumable.
Question: If the meaning is as you have stated, why is it said that clothing is capable of receiving perfuming?
Answer: Clothing, too, is merely a conceptual construct.
It is not truly capable of being perfumed;
this is known because,
as when a garment is perfumed with incense, it is the fragrance of the garment that remains.
You should know that when silk is perfumed, the fragrance does not permeate the garment;
this serves as proof.
The term "perfuming the robes" is a figurative expression for their location;
it is simply that four *citta-prakṛti* (consciousness-elements) of silk and so forth receive the perfuming.
If one infers by this sequence,
the four objects and so forth are likewise not susceptible to perfuming. Why is this?
When perfumed by incense, the incense becomes [the fragrance]; this is the meaning of "fruit.
This is the principle of cause and effect.
This is precisely the virtue of the Tathāgatagarbha;
apart from the Garbha, there is nothing else.
The reason for knowing this is as follows:
However, among all phenomena, those that distinguish cause and effect are merely provisional gateways for turning toward the truth, not the ultimate reality.
Fourth, as for that which is associated with the perfuming agent:
Only the Tathāgatagarbha possesses the meaning of being the locus for all phenomena;
other dharmas do not.
Why is this? Because it does not maintain its own nature. If that is so, why is this?
It is said that the mirror and the object correspond.
The answer is: the mirror also does not correspond;
rather, the mirror corresponds to the external object.
This is precisely the principle of correct cause and effect.
The principle of correct cause and effect is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature,
it is the suchness of selflessness; thus it is known.
That "the mirror responds to the object" is a metaphorical designation for the principle of transformation.
It clarifies the meaning of the two causes that give rise to the seven kinds of luminosity.
It is realized that there is only the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
If this is elucidated through its causal significance,
it constitutes two kinds of causes.
First is the cause of production;
second is the cause of projection.
It is like a person shooting an arrow.
Releasing the arrow is the generative cause;
drawing the bow is the inducing cause;
this continues until the production of the karmic fruit and the end of life.
This is the cause of production (*janana-hetu*).
The continuity of withering and death is the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Because these two kinds of causes cannot be established apart from the ālayavijñāna.
There is only consciousness.
The eight internal [bases] serve as the foundation for the external;
this is the realization that there is only consciousness.
This is how it is known:
because all things are consciousness, this is the fundamental basis.
External phenomena depend upon consciousness to arise; lacking inherent substance, they are empty.
You should know that consciousness is the fundamental source of these dharmas;
other dharmas are falsely constructed and cannot be relied upon.
Regarding the ninth stage, the fruition of wisdom:
through the practices of hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
one progresses from the subtle to the manifest.
Furthermore, it is established by means of the fundamental consciousness,
the Tathāgatagarbha; for this reason,
one knows that the perfuming of hearing flows from True Suchness (tathatā).
It should be known that suchness is the basis of the three kinds of wisdom;
it receives perfuming and thereby forms seeds.
The attainment of supremacy is transformed, while other dharmas do not exist [in that way].
Question: If this is so, then True Suchness possesses all virtues and flows forth from itself alone.
Why is it necessary for further perfuming?
The answer is: True Suchness (tathatā) does not maintain its own nature;
because it arises only by depending on conditions, it is said to be "perfumed."
Tenth, regarding enjoyment:
dependent origination and consciousness rely upon one another to form a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
Only then can one experience [objects],
thereby clarifying that there is only consciousness (vijñaptimātra).
If there were no ālayavijñāna to grasp and sustain these experiences, [such experience would be impossible].
Since that which arises through conditions cannot constitute experience,
the treatise states:
"All phenomena reside within the storehouse consciousness."
It is the same for consciousness with respect to phenomena.
These two are mutually causes for one another,
and they are also constantly mutual effects.
This verse speaks in terms of the sphere of enjoyment of the subsequent mind (*pṛṣṭhacitta*).
Regarding the meaning of "enjoyment," as the treatise states:
one explanation names it "object-condition consciousness" (*ālambana-vijñāna*).
The second is called the consciousness of feeling (*vedanā-vijñāna*).
To discern feeling is termed "discrimination," which gives rise to mental factors such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
This constitutes experience (*upabhoga*).
The universal [defilements] establish the seeds and the manifest [defilements];
they all produce, lead, and establish,
thereby achieving non-futility.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the treatise.
Seventh, regarding the presence or absence of causes and conditions: the ālayavijñāna.
They arise solely through mutual causality;
there are no other causes.
Other phenomena are not like this.
The twelvefold dependent origination pertains solely to the experience of rebirth through dominant influence. Regarding dependent origination,
there are three types of dependent origination.
That is to say: the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*). Why is this so?
Answer: Because of the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth.
These are its provisional characteristics;
because they are explained according to specific phenomena,
their conditions are not the same as those of the ālayavijñāna.
Rational analysis does not speak on the basis of actual entities;
it speaks only in terms of the initial gateway of origination,
describing how things mutually function as cause and effect.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
Furthermore, according to the secret [teaching],
all possess four conditions.
The eighth assembly is titled "Returning to Orthodoxy to Clarify that the Ālaya-vijñāna Exists.
The Liang translation of the treatise states:
"Furthermore, regarding those within the True Dharma..."
Although one may aspire to and delight in selflessness, thereby opposing the view of a personal body (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
there nevertheless remains within the ālayavijñāna a self-love (ātmasneha).
The commentary states:
The previous section concerned those outside the Buddha-dharma;
this present section concerns those within the Buddha-dharma.
There are three categories:
first, that which pertains to right reflection;
second, that which pertains to right cultivation.
Three are in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
Among these three types of persons,
two have suppressed the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
One person eliminates the view of self.
Why? Because the previous two persons infer the absence of self through comparison.
Furthermore, because one person realizes the absence of self,
it is said that this contradicts the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Having long practiced the attachment to a self,
even though it contradicts the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
[it persists] within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
My craving continues to pursue me constantly;
therefore, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is not a locus for such attachment.
If one takes the name *ālaya* and explains it according to its meaning of *liya* (clinging/attachment), [then the view of a self would indeed be a locus of attachment].
Thus it is the most supreme.
Now, based on this meaning,
we shall discuss the name "ālaya."
If it refers solely to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
its meaning is superior; however,
if it is intended to designate the locus for the two views of self— namely, the self of persons and the self of phenomena— then [the former interpretation] is more appropriate.
Thus, it is not superior.
The meaning of *ālaya* should be understood according to this principle.
The establishment of the ālayavijñāna based on the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* consists of nineteen sections.
The first is: "The karma performed and accumulated in previous lives. The commentary states:
Consciousness has the sense of being prior to all phenomena.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says:
"Because it is always present at the forefront at all times."
Regarding the statement that "the two delusions act as conditions," the commentary explains:
because consciousness serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for all phenomena.

Regarding the statement that "the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-vāsanā*) from beginningless time act as the cause," the commentary explains: [that these are the causal condition].
The seeds of habitual tendencies from beginningless conceptual proliferation serve as the cause for the initial arising of consciousness.
4. "That which is produced from all seeds. The commentary states:
This clarifies that the seeds of all phenomena are produced by consciousness.
5. "Having the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) as its essence. The commentary states:
Based upon the various seeds and the manifesting consciousnesses of the higher mind,
it functions as maturation in the present; therefore, it takes this maturation as its essence.
6. This consciousness is able to grasp and maintain [the body].

The commentary states: It clarifies that this fundamental consciousness is one with all phenomena, and all phenomena are likewise one with the fundamental consciousness, just as clarified butter and its container are identical.
7. The discernment of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya-vijñapti*). The commentary states:
Consciousness sustains the various material sense-faculties, causing them to be clear and distinct.
8. The locus of the sense-faculties (*indriyāśraya-deśa*). The commentary states:
Consciousness serves as the basis for the various faculties, thereby constituting their supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*).

Regarding the phrase "the nine and the perfumation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-vāsanā*)," the commentary explains that it clarifies that consciousness serves as the locus of support for the seeds of the mental states (*adhicaitta-bīja*) perfumed by conceptual proliferation.
"10. At all times, its uniform arising and ceasing cannot be discerned. The commentary explains:
This clarifies that the continuity of that fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) arises free from all conceptualization;
it cannot be known through discursive discrimination.
Eleventh, furthermore, it can grasp and discern the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). The commentary states:
