it is explained as in the lower section of the sutra.
If one refers to the Final Teaching (Jōgyō), however...
All things are suchness.
If one considers them from the perspective of the One Vehicle,
it is as explained above.
This is what is designated by the Perfect Teaching (Eṇḍen-gyō) and points toward the One Vehicle;
it is precisely the skillful means (upāya) of the One Vehicle.
It is subsumed within the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Within the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma" (*Fameng pin*), the scope of the benefits and harms of understanding and practice is determined by universally relying upon the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). Indeed, the intent behind the arising of the Tathāgata’s teaching is for the sake of sentient beings.
Due to the varying capacities of sentient beings— whether shallow or deep—
the teachings consequently form two types.
The first is the teaching of distinct characteristics (biphasa-dharmaparyāya).
Second, the gate of common and distinct teachings.
The teaching of distinct characteristics refers to the differentiation between the characteristics of good and evil;
it is intended to lead beginners into correct understanding so that they do not fall into error.
This refers to matters such as the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome actions; by analogy with these,
the meaning can be understood.
Second, regarding the teachings of both common and uncommon [vehicles]:
these are also called the "secret teachings" within the sūtras.
As for why they arose:
Because sentient beings possess deeply ingrained afflictions and boundless, artful, and slippery false wisdom through their calculations,
the Teaching was established in order to remedy this malady.
Regarding the characteristics of loss and gain: take,
for example, the great gate of upholding the precepts of the five vehicles,
beginning from the levels of humans and devas upward.
Not yet having attained it constitutes a loss;
having attained it constitutes a benefit;
progressing toward it constitutes a benefit.
To abide [in them] is itself a detriment.
This applies equally to all vehicles.
The practice of one person is thus;
the same applies to the practices of all who have attained liberation.
Furthermore, this is called "accomplishing practice through names."
To seek renown for the sake of the world is detrimental;
to seek renown for the sake of the supramundane is beneficial.
This applies even to all forms of understanding and practice.
One should understand this by analogy as well.
Furthermore, to practice for the sake of profit is to bring harm to the benefit of the world.
That which is for the sake of supramundane benefit is precisely what is beneficial;
this should be understood accordingly even up to all stages of understanding and practice.
Furthermore, one practices for the sake of self-righteousness;
through worldly self-righteousness, one is diminished,
while through supramundane self-righteousness, one is benefited.
This applies to all stages of practice up to the stage of "conduct through understanding";
one should understand them all accordingly.
It is the same for others as well.
Furthermore, one practices for the sake of delighting in worldly existence;
yet while it benefits sentient beings who remain in existence,
it causes harm to oneself remaining in existence.
This applies to all stages of practice and realization;
one should understand them accordingly.
Furthermore, they do not seek fame or profit, nor do they assert their own views while disparaging others, nor do they take pleasure in the existence of the three realms.
There is also loss and gain:
not seeking the name of a Buddha constitutes loss;
not seeking worldly fame constitutes gain.
Even down to such things as not seeking worldly profit or benefit,
all possess both harm and benefit;
one should understand this accordingly.
Furthermore, from the initial teachings upward, non-conceptualization is beneficial while conceptualization is detrimental;
this remains true even regarding the doctrines and meanings of the One Vehicle.
One should understand other cases by analogy as well.
For instance, a single category such as the great observance of precepts possesses such benefits and harms.

Great diligence, great repentance, great non-discrimination between right and wrong, great lack of self-righteousness and disdain for others, great recitation, and great practice through understanding—
all such cases are to be judged according to this principle. Furthermore,
regarding all benefits and harms pertaining to the various vehicles, their practices, principles, and phenomena:
Furthermore, these serve as gateways for benefit and harm for those in the world who have not yet transcended it;
they do not pertain to those who have transcended the world.
As the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya) of the Liang dynasty states:
If it is a mundane phenomenon (*laukika-dharma*), it can be destroyed;
if it is a supramundane phenomenon (*lokottara-dharma*), it cannot be destroyed.
Question: The principles regarding phenomena that cause harm or benefit are clearly established.
Why, then, do you now speak of "defamation" and "non-defamation"?
Answer: The characteristics of harm and benefit are distinct, and their principles do not intermingle.
Now, in order to resolve that previous doubt, there are two types [of cases].
First, for one who possesses false wisdom, there is the answer by way of concealment;
second, for one who possesses correct wisdom, there is the answer by way of manifestation.
Now, this is an answer by way of concealment.
In order to resolve that previous doubt,
it is stated generally as "defaming.
Furthermore, this is said with reference to both the time when a Buddha appears in the world and the time of the final age.
One must determine their conduct and practice.
The characteristics of good and evil are likewise not fixed;
if one speaks of the Buddha’s era, it was characterized by an abundance of goodness.
It is true that evil is prevalent in the final age; this may well be so.
Furthermore, regarding the determination of whether a teaching is heterodox or orthodox based on the two types of capacities—superior and inferior—this too is not fixed.
If one considers both what is encompassed and what is not encompassed,
this can indeed be accepted.
"Encompassed" refers to that which brings about benefit.
If one falls short, a loss is incurred;
this applies accordingly to all subsequent lower levels as well,
just as with the similarities and differences regarding gain and loss within the wholesome.
The same principle may be applied to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
by reversing this application, the meaning is established.
What has been explained above is taught according to the common teaching of the Three Vehicles. If,
however, one considers the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle:
The increase and decrease are infinite. Why is this?
Because the meaning of the One Vehicle is distinct for each, according to conditions.
It is inexhaustible because it cannot be fully explained.
Furthermore, the meaning of "diminution and benefit" encompasses both good and evil;
within the good, there is further good.
Within the wholesome there is the unwholesome;
that which is wholesome within the wholesome is as described in the preceding section on the gates of benefit.
That which is non-virtuous within the virtuous is as described above in the section on harm.
That which is evil within the evil is—
The former refers to those who, by reversing their previous course, act contrary to reason and are unwholesome;
the latter refers to those who, within their evil,
employ skillful means to turn away from evil and thereby establish wholesome roots.
The two meanings of good and evil are equal in their capacity for harm and benefit.
Furthermore, there are two gates regarding the harm and benefit of good and evil.
It is subtle and profound.
Why? Because the karmic capacities and inclinations for defilement and purification among sentient beings are inexhaustible.
To speak briefly now:
we shall discuss only whether one knows or does not know, and whether one avoids or does not avoid.
If one knows yet does not avoid, [it is a fault].
It is difficult for one who avoids [the truth] without knowing it.
Regarding the Chapter on the Two Kinds of Adornments:
"Adornment" refers to the cultivation of virtues that serve as the equipment for a person; thus, it is called adornment.
There are two kinds of difference:
first, merit; second, wisdom.
That which provides nourishment and moisture is called merit; the efficacy of providing such nourishment and moisture is its function.
That which is called "merit" (puṇya) is named "wisdom" (jñāna) when it illuminates principles;
that which is "penetrating observation" is named "insight" (prajñā).
There are four meanings for "adornment" (vyūha).
First, that which can support the person is called adornment;
second, that which can support the mind is called adornment;
third, that which can support the fruit is called adornment.
Fourth, the adornment of the level characteristic of all conditioned phenomena;
it is also called discipline (*vinaya*) and also called the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
It is also called the practice that assists the Path.
This meaning pertains to the Three Vehicles;
however, it is not fully complete in the Lesser Vehicle.
It speaks only of the gateway of wisdom;
it also possesses auxiliary merit that brings fulfillment,
yet this is not praised within the teachings.
Within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
both types of adornment are fully praised.
Within the teachings of the One Vehicle, there are ten adornments.
As explained in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātunirdeśa*) of the sutra, other meanings are as discussed in separate chapters.
Regarding the meaning of the Three Jewels (*Triratna*), this is the Chapter on the Meaning of the Three Jewels. As for the meaning of the Three Jewels:
Third is the number.
"Jewel" (ratna) carries the meaning of being precious.
It enables practitioners to transcend birth and death and attain supreme enlightenment.
That which is worthy of esteem is called a "jewel" (ratna).
This refers to the meaning of the Triple Gem— Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—
which, in brief, consists of three types.
First, the Three Treasures of Common Characteristics;
second, the Three Treasures of Distinct Characteristics;
third, the Three Treasures of Sustaining Presence.
Regarding the Three Jewels of Identical Character (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa):
it means that within the single dharmatā of true suchness (tathatā), there are three distinct meanings.
Because these consist of the meaning of awakening (bodhi), the meaning of the guiding dharma (dharma), and the meaning of the harmonious community (saṃgha), they are called the Three Jewels.
Regarding the second, the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*):
"Buddha" signifies the sense of being venerable within the context of conditions.
This refers to the various bodies, such as the two bodies, one body, three bodies, four bodies, ten bodies, and so forth, which are common to the world.
As distinguished in the section on questions and answers:
"Dharma" refers to principle, teaching, practice, fruit, and the inexhaustible meanings of the teachings, and so forth.
"Saṃgha" refers to those with outflows and those without outflows, the maintenance of the precepts through ritual acts (karmavācanā), and the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and mahāsattvas.
There are two kinds of the Three Jewels as maintained through physical representation (*saṃsthāna-saṃghāra*):
first, those represented by form (*lakṣaṇa-saṃsthāra*),
namely Buddhas depicted in painting, carved in sandalwood, and so forth.
The second refers to dharmas such as paper, silk, speech, and sound;
the third refers to the Saṃgha, including those with outflows and those without outflows, such as those who have shaved their heads and wear the kāṣāya.
These two principles constitute the maintenance [of the Dharma].
That is to say, the dharmatā-tathatā serves as the basis for both ordinary beings and sages:
first, as the basis for birth; second, as the basis for the objective sphere.
The establishment of names and principles through material support is termed "abiding support" (zhuchi).
The Three Jewels pervade the five teachings;
the first exists within the world.
Second, the training of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
third, the training of bodhisattvas taught through gradual instruction;
fourth, the training of bodhisattvas taught through sudden instruction.
The meaning of the first, the study of the universal conduct, realization, vision, hearing, and so forth of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Samantabhadra,
may be understood by analogy.
As for the characteristics of the Three Jewels of the One Vehicle:
As stated in the sutra,
there are briefly ten gateways.
First, the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
They teach and transform sentient beings,
causing them to resolve upon bodhicitta;
for this reason, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted.
Second, they reveal the profound and wondrous treasury of all dharmas;
therefore, they are able to ensure that the jewel of the Dharma is never interrupted.
Third, they fully possess and uphold the teachings on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Therefore, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.
Fourth, they are further able to praise all great vows;
therefore, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted.
Fifth, by analytically explaining the twelve links of dependent origination,
one is thus able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
Sixth, one practices the six forms of harmonious respect.
Therefore, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is never interrupted.
Seventh, they further plant the seeds of the Buddha within the field of sentient beings,
causing the sprouts of perfect enlightenment to grow.
Therefore, they are able to ensure that the Jewel of the Buddha is never interrupted.
Eighth, they protect and uphold the Three Jewels without begrudging their own bodies or lives.
Therefore, he is able to ensure that the Jewel of the Dharma is not interrupted.
Ninth, he skillfully guides the assembly with a mind free from anxiety or affliction;
therefore, he is able to ensure that the Jewel of the Sangha is not interrupted.
The True Dharma taught by the Buddhas of the past, future,
and present is not contravened;
therefore, it is able to ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
These thirteen jewels are subsumed within the teaching of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Why is this? Because they possess the characteristics of the thirteen jewels.
In the realization of the mind through practice,
there is nothing that does not manifest within the sphere of scriptural knowledge;
this is precisely what it means to abide in and maintain [the teaching].
This brings about great benefit.
The reason for speaking of ten is the desire to manifest their immeasurability.
This penetration pertains to the Indra and Subtle Abodes;
the two vehicles and the Small Vehicle do not possess these characteristics.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on the Sixfold Concordant Reverence (*ṣaḍ-sāmīcī*):
the sixfold concordant reverence refers to the sameness of physical action, verbal action, and mental action; the sameness of precepts (*śīla*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and training (*śikṣā*).
This is also called "sameness of benefit.
Since their precepts and views are identical,
their physical and vocal actions are likewise entirely the same.
Because there is no discord or contention, it is called "harmonious respect.
This meaning applies to the Hīnayāna, the Triyāna, and the Ekayāna alike.
As for the Hīnayāna that adheres to the literal teaching:
According to the facts, patience and compassion are based on [the realization of] phenomena;
if one follows the initial teachings of the Three Vehicles,
patience and compassion rely on emptiness.
If one relies on the Final Teaching (Jiao), because one knows that self and others are equal and of one suchness, one gives rise to patience and compassion;
this relies upon the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching,
which is superior to the dharmas of the three vehicles and above.
Because this is a skillful means and because it is that which is being pointed toward,
it belongs to the One Vehicle.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter Four: The Fourth Assembly, Chapter on the Accumulation of Flowers, Section on the Initial Establishment of the Ten Pāramitās. Regarding the ten pāramitās: [text continues].
These are the ten practices of the stages of conduct (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*):
first, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*);
second, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Third, the perfection of patience;
fourth, the perfection of diligence;
fifth, the perfection of meditative concentration.
Sixth, the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Seventh, the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā).
Eighth, the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
The ninth is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*).
The tenth is the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
These are the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
Because giving alone brings joy to both oneself and others,
it is called the "practice of joy"; because ethical discipline accomplishes the benefit of both oneself and others, [it is called the practice of benefit].
The second is called the practice of benefiting others,
because through patience one achieves freedom from anger and resentment toward both oneself and others.
The third is called the practice of being without malice or resentment.
Because diligence accomplishes supreme virtues,
it is the fourth, called "Inexhaustible Conduct.
Because the dhyāna-pāramitā is characterized by tranquility, [it is the fifth].
The fifth is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion,
because the wisdom of realization regarding dependent origination is manifest before one.
The sixth is called the practice of "Well-Appearing" (Sudṛśa).
It is called the seventh, the practice of non-attachment, because through skillful means one accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others,
and because one attains mastery over one's vows, being able to accomplish them at will.
The eighth is called the practice of reverence,
because it brings sentient beings to maturity through the attainment of superior power and mastery.
The ninth is called the practice of wholesome dharmas.
The activities of the three karmas for the benefit of others are not in vain;
for they act according to what they have taught,
and teach according to how they have acted.
The tenth is called "true practice.
Because it initiates and performs [action], it has the meaning of "practice" (*caryā*).
This meaning applies to all three vehicles.
It does not accord with the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
In the Initial Teaching, all is emptiness;
in the Final Teaching, all is suchness.
That which is indicated by the teaching of the One Vehicle is a skillful means;
furthermore, these are enumerated as ten to manifest their immeasurability.
This is subsumed within the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Question: What is the difference between the ten numbers of the Three Vehicles and those of the One Vehicle?
Answer: Regarding the ten numbers of the Three Vehicles:
Adapting to the transformative methods according to various regions,
there is no separate standard dharma;
one relies instead upon the teaching of the One Vehicle.
There is another corresponding method.
Furthermore, one should know that this occurs while remaining within that very samādhi.
The distinctions between them are entirely different;
this should be understood.
Other meanings are found in separate chapters.

Regarding the chapter on establishing the One Vehicle, Three Vehicles, and Hīnayāna scriptural treasuries within the Ten Treasury Collections: based upon the Hīnayāna of those who follow the teachings of the ignorant.
The meaning of the "Three Baskets" (Tripitaka) is twofold.
The first is the Three Baskets themselves,
namely the Sūtra-piṭaka.
It is also called *sūtra* and also called *sūtrānta*.
Second is the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
The three Piṭakas;
and the two Piṭakas,
namely the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka.
The names of these are the same as those of the Three Vehicles,
but their meanings differ.
The substance of the Tripitaka of the Hīnayāna is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering.
The three vehicles and the three piṭakas are subsumed within the nature of reality (*tattva*).
These three vehicles and piṭakas consist of five types.
The first is the single piṭaka.
That is, the Mātṛkā-piṭaka.
Second, the two piṭakas:
namely, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Third, the three collections (tripiṭaka),
namely Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya. Fourth,
the four collections (catuḥpiṭaka).
That is to say, by adding the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*,
there are five *piṭakas*.
That is to say, by adding the *Dhāraṇī-mantra-piṭaka*.
The doctrinal meanings of the One Vehicle are all different,
namely what are called the Ten Treasuries (daśapiṭaka).

1. The treasury of faith, 2. the treasury of ethical discipline, 3. the treasury of self-respect, 4. the treasury of moral dread, 5. the treasury of learning, 6. the treasury of generosity, 7. the treasury of wisdom, 8. the treasury of right mindfulness, 9. the treasury of retention, and 10. the treasury of eloquence. Question: The meaning of these three treasuries is fundamentally based upon the teachings.
The meaning of the ten *piṭakas* encompasses their doctrinal significance.
How, then, are the ten *piṭakas* correlated with the three *piṭakas*? Answer:
The three vehicles and the Lesser Vehicle are explained according to the distinctions of their respective spheres of activity.
The teaching is not itself the meaning;
the meaning of the One Vehicle takes the teaching as its teaching.
Furthermore, it is taught by means of its meaning;
within the meanings of the Three Vehicles,
this very meaning already exists.
How much more so for the One Vehicle;
this meaning is as explained in a separate chapter.
Regarding the six unconditioned phenomena in the "Chapter on the Six Unconditioned Phenomena": the six unconditioned phenomena are...

First, space; second, nirvāṇa; third, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); fourth, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); fifth, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); and sixth, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Question:
For what reason are the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas of the One Vehicle enumerated in the same way as those of the Three Vehicles?
Answer: This meaning is extremely profound;
it is explained below in numerical form to make it easier for people to believe.
This is explained in detail in the commentaries.
Regarding what is taught in the Hīnayāna, the Initial Teaching, the Final Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching:
it is the unconditioned, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, tranquility, freedom from thought, cessation, and the ineffable.
Such meanings as these are all entirely different when the various vehicles are compared with one another.
They also vary in depth, shallowness, breadth, and narrowness,
such as the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the three unconditioned phenomena, the three emptinesses, the eight emptinesses, up to the eighteen emptinesses, and so forth;
that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty.
This is because they are based on different enumerations of names;
thus, they cannot be reconciled into one,
existing only within the single gateway of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).
All that exists, whether being or non-being, shares a single characteristic:
namely, the characteristic of signlessness (*animitta*).
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter on the Three Realms: Regarding the three realms, they are the locations where sentient beings receive their retributive fruits and undergo the segmentation of existence;
these are divided into three distinct categories.
From the Avīci Hell up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, male and female beings dwell together,
and there is an abundance of defiled desire;
therefore, it is called the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
From the Brahma heavens of the first dhyāna up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
there are no female forms,
nor is there any defilement of desire.
The palaces are lofty and vast;
they are born through transformation from form,
and are therefore called the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
From the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception,
there are only four states of mind and no material form; therefore,
it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Within these three realms,
there are four types of distinctions regarding the coarse and subtle, the emerging and the submerging, among ordinary beings and sages.
First, the three realms of segmented existence resulting from bound karma;
second, the three realms of segmented existence resulting from unbound karma;
third, the three realms of transformational existence resulting from residual habit-energies.
Fourth, not abandoning the world of transformation within the three realms.
Question: Since both transformation and not abandoning the world are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, for what reason do they remain within the three realms?
Answer: The transformation body and other forms remain in the world out of compassion,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Because they can enter the world again through great compassion, they remain within the three realms.
Within these three realms, [they dwell].
The celestial realms of the Great Division consist of twenty-eight:
six in the desire realm and eighteen in the form realm.
Excluding the Bṛhatphala Heaven and including the Āsaṃjñika Heaven,
they constitute eighteen.
The formless realm has four [levels].
Among these, their meanings, characteristics, names, numbers, coarseness,
and subtlety are all different.
One should know that the meanings of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles,
and the Lesser Vehicle are all distinct from one another.
As in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The Yāma Heaven,
the Tuṣita Heaven,
and the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven,
the Brahmā Heaven,
and the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
The Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā,
the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā,
and the Heaven of Mahābrahmā.
Ābhāsvara Heaven,
Parīttābha Heaven,
and Apramāṇābha Heaven.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven,
the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
and the Parīttaśubha Heaven.
The Heaven of Immeasurable Purity,
the Heaven of Universal Purity,
and the Heaven of Secret Body.
The Limited Secret Body Heaven,
the Immeasurable Secret Body Heaven,
and the Secret Fruit Heaven.
In this context, the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva),
the Heaven Free from Affliction (avṛha), and the Heaven Free from Heat (atapā) are not included.
The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven,
the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven,
and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
The devas of the sphere of infinite space,
the devas of the sphere of infinite consciousness,
and the devas of the sphere of nothingness.
The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;
adding these four heavens,
there are thirty-two heavens in total.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"From the Avīci Hell up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception,
all beings therein— whether coarse or subtle— "
Arranged in successive layers with no intervening space, for this reason,
it is impossible to describe the boundaries of a certain class of sentient beings.
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"This land is eternally peaceful and secure.
One should know this.
Within the three realms there are sentient beings, both coarse and subtle.
The coarse perceive the destruction of the kalpa;
the subtle remain ever secure.
The reason the Buddha does not teach in the same way is that he wishes to manifest the inexhaustibility of the realm of sentient beings,
as well as meanings such as those concerning Indra and the subtle.
In all cases, these are not the same.
In the Hīnayāna, the three realms are identical in that they are destroyed by a single catastrophe.
In the Initial Teaching, the meaning of the three realms is that they are empty.
In the Final Teaching, the three realms are identical to suchness and are without discrimination;
in the One Vehicle, the three realms are what is called inexhaustible and without discrimination.
Other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Regarding the fourfold analysis of the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*):

the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence consists of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of ready speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Knowledge that cognizes names is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
The wisdom that knows meanings is called the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
The eloquence regarding speech and sounds is called the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
Causing others to delight in speaking is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
It is called "unimpeded" because it penetrates all things without obstruction;
its essence is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
If one considers this according to the Hīnayāna:
The four unhindered analytical knowledges (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) constitute its actual wisdom;
in the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, that wisdom is emptiness (śūnyatā).
If one reaches the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), that wisdom is suchness;
if one reaches the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), it is the forty kinds of non-obstruction,
as explained in the ninth stage of the sutra below.
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) are based on ten types of distinctions.
First, they are based on specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Second, based on the characteristic of sameness;
third, based on the characteristic of practice;
fourth, based on the characteristic of exposition.
Fifth, the characteristic based on wisdom;
sixth, the characteristic based on the absence of conceit;
seventh, the characteristic based on the distinction between the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna.
8. Based on the characteristics of the Bodhisattva stage;
9. Based on the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage;
10. Based on the characteristics of performing and maintaining [the teachings].
The latter five are the marks of purity;
this is distinguished according to the teachings.
If, however, one relies on their actual qualities:
This is precisely the inexhaustible eloquence within the gateway of Samantabhadra.
Other meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.
Regarding the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakṣa), there are three types of factors of enlightenment.
First, the category of the Śrāvaka path;
those who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] are likewise included here.
Second, the category of the direct-advancing path.
That is to say, there are only the six pāramitās;
and thirdly, the categories of the path of the One Vehicle,
namely, the inexhaustible categories of the path.
The names of the categories of the Path (mārga-varga) in the Hīnayāna are the same as those in the Initial Teaching for those who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna]. Why is this?
Because the aspects of seeing and cultivation are not distinct in these two cases,
although the names do not differ,
their meanings are entirely different.
The factors of the path in the Hīnayāna exist only within contemplation;
those of the Mahāyāna [exist]...
Their contemplation extends outward;
furthermore, their principle and wisdom are distinct,
as is the case with the śrāvaka path-factors (mārgāṅga) of the Hīnayāna.
The wisdom of the selflessness of persons is for the sake of turning the mind toward the factors of enlightenment;
the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena is for the sake of [realizing] the Dharma.
Question: Why are the *bodhipakṣa-dharmas* (factors conducive to awakening) for those who proceed directly not the same as those for those who have turned their minds [from the Lesser Vehicle]?
Answer: The *bodhipakṣa-dharmas* for those who have turned their minds are intended to attract those of the "Dharma of the Ignorant" (*bāla-dharman*) within the Lesser Vehicle.
Their names are the same as those of the Śrāvakas.
If one were to directly advance as a Bodhisattva while remaining identical to the Śrāvakas, their conceptual discrimination would only increase further.
It was omitted because it would have been incongruous with the underlying principle.
As for the "Dharmas of the Path" (Mārga-aṅga):
first are the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
These refer to body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
As for the four right efforts:
they concern evil that has not yet arisen.
One employs skillful means to prevent unarisen [unwholesome states] from arising, and employs skillful means to sever those that have already arisen.
One employs skillful means to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen,
and [to increase] those wholesome states that have already arisen.
One employs skillful means to cause them to increase.
As for the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), they are:
the concentration of desire, the concentration of energy, the concentration of mindfulness, and the concentration of wisdom.
The five faculties (pañcendriyāṇi) are:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
The five powers (pañcabalāni) are:
These are the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
The seven factors of enlightenment are:

the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of rapture, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view,
right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration;
its essence is subsumed within ten factors.
This refers to the factors of enlightenment consisting of faith, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, joy, tranquility, equanimity, volition, ethical discipline, and concentration.
Faith is divided into two:
the faculty of faith and the power of faith.
The factor of diligence is eightfold;
that is, the four right efforts constitute the four roots of diligence and the power of diligence.
The awakening factor of diligence, right effort,
and mindfulness are divided into four.
These are the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
The factors of wisdom consist of eight:
the four foundations of mindfulness constitute four of them.
The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, and right view constitute [the aggregate of wisdom].
Joy constitutes the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Serenity constitutes the factor of enlightenment of serenity.
Equanimity is the factor of enlightenment called equanimity;
volition is a constituent of enlightenment,
namely right intention.
The precepts are divided into three:
namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Samādhi is concentration.
Concentration is divided into eight types, namely:
the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*),

the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
The knowledge of the exhaustion [of outflows] and the knowledge of non-arising constitute bodhi.
Because they accord with those dharmas and possess superior power and function, they are called "aids to the path" (bodhipakṣa).
This is also acceptable.
The Mahāyāna aids to the path should be established according to their respective natures;
they are not subsumed by way of these ten meanings.
Why is this? Because the conditions for arising are distinct.
This refers to the Bodhisattva who proceeds directly forward.
The six pāramitās are employed as the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga).
The six practices that reach the fruit are called pāramitās;
the six practices that assist toward the fruit are called factors of the path.
Those who proceed directly and those who turn their minds are both distinct from the śrāvakas. Why is this?
Because the factors of the path are themselves emptiness,
the ultimate teaching (zhōngjiào) is identical to suchness,
the path-factors of the One Vehicle.
This refers to the two thousand answers in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (Lokottara-parivarta) of the sutra's later sections.
This is known because [the Buddha] again questioned [Subhūti] regarding the dharmas of practice within that "Chapter on Leaving the World."
Furthermore, the meaning within the text consists entirely of words of exhortation;
since these are the vows and practices of Samantabhadra, [one should practice them].
It is vast and boundless;
even the factors of the path cannot be found as something slight.
Such is the ultimate meaning that returns to this.
This is explained in detail in a separate chapter.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures," the first division, *sūtra*,
is called "thread" (*sūtra*) in this land.
It is also called "Sūtra" and also called "Fountain.
As for the *Geyasūtra*:
This is called the *Ge-yong jing* (Verses in Pairs Sutra).
*Gāthā* means "sutra of non-repeated verses."
Vaipulya means "Extensive Sūtra.
Vyākaraṇa means "Sūtra of Prophecy" (授記經). Udāna means...
