Third, if one sees a bhikṣu who keeps a wife and children,
and speaks of his faults according to one's own whims, one commits a grave offense.
Fourth, if one sees a person who is grieving and wishes to take their own life...
To increase another's anger through one's own intent,
or to destroy another's life-faculty, constitutes a grave offense.
Fifth, to take wealth or treasures from a deserted road constitutes a grave offense.
Sixth, if one sees another wishing to take a life and praises them with flattering words,
thereby inciting their anger, one commits a grave offense.
Seventh, if one sees others intending to burn down a monastic dwelling and does not admonish them with all one's heart,
one commits a grave offense. Eighth, if one sees or hears that another has committed a grave offense.
If one does not go three times to summon [the offender] and instruct them to repent, it constitutes a grave offense.
Ninth, if one sees someone committing the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) and fails to reprimand them or urge them to abandon such actions, it constitutes a grave offense.
Tenth, to see or hear that another is about to undertake a great act of virtue,
yet to give rise to anger and destroy their endeavor, constitutes a grave offense.
Eleventh, to see another who is addicted to food and fond of wine...
One should go and rebuke them with one's own feelings, except in cases where one has committed a grave offense due to one's own circumstances.
Twelfth: seeing someone committing adultery with another's wife.
To speak of another’s husband constitutes a grave offense.
Thirteenth: regarding another’s enemy, to form the perception of them being an enemy constitutes a grave offense.
Fourteenth: seeing another regard an enemy as an infant;
how could one speak of regarding such a person as an infant while committing a grave offense?
Fifteenth: seeing others engaged in a brawl.
To assist in striking with a mallet constitutes a grave offense.
Sixteenth: seeing another person in a state of concealment or hiding, to speak of it to others and cause them great anger constitutes a grave offense.
Seventeenth: Upon seeing or hearing of another’s virtuous deeds, to say that one has not performed them at all constitutes a grave offense.
Eighteenth: Walking upon a desolate road.
To see others constructing stūpas and temples or building vihāras, and yet not assist them, constitutes a grave offense. Nineteenth:
to see or hear that someone has distanced themselves from virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and is associating with evil companions.
To praise what is good without encouraging its relinquishment constitutes a grave offense.
Twenty: [entering] the homes of caṇḍālas, the dwellings of evil persons, the homes of fierce dogs, or the abodes of śrāvakas and followers of the two vehicles.
If one goes to attend to one's own urgent affairs, one commits a grave offense.
Twenty-first: if one sees, hears, or suspects that an animal was killed, yet forms the perception that it was not seen, heard, or suspected, and eats this meat, one commits a grave offense.
Twenty-second: to kill while seeing, hearing, or suspecting [the victim], yet to claim one did not see, hear, or suspect it;
if one does not eat such meat, one commits a grave offense.
Twenty-third: to understand skillful means and know the faculties of sentient beings.
If one claims that failing to speak out constitutes a grave offense,
this is the twenty-fourth [point]: one must never speak to others about having seen various bodhisattvas or any other such visions.
In their present life, they encounter obstacles to the Path and contract leprosy;
at times they are deluded,
and at times they are afflicted with cataracts or blindness.
At times, when the eyes are blurred, one falsely discriminates among all phenomena and inevitably falls into delusion.
Second is the clarification of the sphere of guarding the precepts.
This is explained in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.
Regarding the ten wholesome dharmas precepts of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Question—how does this precept differ [from others]?
Answer: According to the characteristics of the precepts, there are also distinctions;
twenty-four precepts are received by beginners.
They are also entrusted to laypeople.
The ten inexhaustible precepts exist prior to attaining the [monastic] stage and apply to both monastics and laity.
The four pārājika precepts pertain to those who have gone forth directly;
they are for renunciants.
I have briefly sent this letter to part ways.
Based on their faculties and conduct,
it may also be said that the benefit [of these teachings] is universal.
The precepts of the ten wholesome dharmas are entrusted to the ten stages;
they consist of seeing, hearing, and cultivation.
This interpretation is also consistent with the meaning.
Furthermore, these ten precepts of wholesome conduct are natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and do not involve a separate rite of formal undertaking.
Based on this, its meaning may also be considered as pertaining to the higher realms;
it encompasses those who follow the Wheel-Turning King’s transformation of the mundane world,
and thus it also extends to the lower realms.
Although the name applies universally,
the meaning is specific; that is to say,
it refers to the universal arising of the precepts.
This principle does not apply to the Hīnayāna of those who follow the dharma of the ignorant.
If it concerns Śrāvakas who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna],
then regarding the distinctions between their precepts— whether they are identical or different, common or uncommon— their training remains the same.
This is explained in detail in the section on the training in ethical discipline (*śīla-śikṣā*) within the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the chapter on the ten paths of unwholesome action (*daśākuśalakarmapatha*):

the ten unwholesome actions are: first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, harsh speech; sixth, divisive speech; seventh, frivolous speech; eighth, covetousness; ninth, malice; and tenth, delusion. These actions are of two kinds.
First, because the nature of unwholesome karma contradicts reason;
second, because the arousal of bad discipline (*dauḥśīlya*) pervades all three types of action (*trikarma*),
and its nature consists of the ten unwholesome paths of action (*daśākuśala*).
There are also both active and non-active [karmas].
Active karma is of three kinds:
that performed by oneself, that performed through instigation, and that performed by rejoicing upon seeing or hearing.
There is one type of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), namely, that which is simultaneous with the act itself (*kriyā-sahabhū-avijñapti*).

Question: Why is it that the unwholesome restraint (*akuśala-saṃvara*) does not likewise consist of non-informative action that co-exists with the physical form (*rūpa-sahabhū-avijñapti*) as is the case within the [wholesome] precepts?

Answer: Regarding the karma of non-restraint (akuśala-saṃvara), there is also the case of one born into a family of non-restraint who, having recognized [the nature of their lineage], goes forth and takes up the instruments of killing;
at that very moment, they obtain non-restraint.
The unwholesome restraint (akuśala-saṃvara) is not produced solely by a formal resolve (*cetanā*) over a long period of time;
because there is this distinct principle,
it does not correspond to the physical form as the wholesome precepts do.
Furthermore, there are those who, by means of a vow, acquire an evil code of discipline (*dauḥśīlya*),
yet this does not apply to everyone.
Moreover, there is a secret reversal that relies upon the ten non-virtues as a basis for goodness.
As the Liang Commentary states:
The treatise says,
"Furthermore, there is a sutra which says:"
How does a bodhisattva practice killing?
It is when a bodhisattva severs the continuity of a sentient being that possesses life.
The commentary states:
If there is life, one knows that there is karma;
if there is karma, one knows that there are afflictions.
Due to the presence of these three,
the continuity of the six realms and four modes of birth remains uninterrupted.
If a bodhisattva, according to their faculties and natures...
For them, he expounds the noble path of the three vehicles,
causing them to practice so as to sever these three dharmas and attain the fruit of nirvana without remainder,
becoming beings who do not undergo rebirth.
This is called taking life because it involves the severing of the life-force.
The treatise asks:
How does a bodhisattva take what has not been given by another?
"If a bodhisattva takes for himself what was not given by another.
The commentary states:
"The bodhisattva embraces all sentient beings through great compassion."
For the sake of their own retinue,
they cause them to leave behind the perilous difficulties of birth and death,
and they seize from others those sentient beings who have not been given to them.
It is called "seized" rather than "given by another" because it was not bestowed by one's parents, a sovereign, or others.
The treatise says:
What is a bodhisattva’s practice of sexual misconduct?
It is when a bodhisattva gives rise to improper thoughts and so forth toward sensual objects.
The commentary states:
The three karmas of a bodhisattva are the opposite of sexual desire; in his mind,
he knows them to be empty, false, and unreal, and the root of all evils.
To speak in such a manner with one's mouth while not acting accordingly with one's body is likewise a contradiction.
This refers to giving rise to improper intentions and so forth regarding sensual objects;
therefore, it is called "practicing sexual misconduct.
The treatise says:
How can a bodhisattva speak what is false?
If a bodhisattva perceives something as false and is able to declare it as false.
[Commentary: This means:
All phenomena are entirely false and illusory.
Because the bodhisattva speaks in accordance with their falsity, he is called "one who can speak";
thus, he is called "one who can speak falsehood."
The treatise says:
What is a bodhisattva’s practice of divisive speech?
It is when a bodhisattva constantly dwells in a state of supreme emptiness and stillness.
The commentary states:
Divisive speech causes discord between this person and that;
the Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness and speaks of emptiness.
One causes oneself and others not to see "this" and "that," let alone to be in harmony; therefore,
it is called the practice of divisive speech.
The treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to abide in *pāruṣya*?
If a bodhisattva abides at the further shore of all that is to be known.
The commentary states:
According to the direct meaning,
the term *pāruṣya* denotes harsh speech.
Those who dwell in harsh speech are not approached by others; the Bodhisattva, however,
dwells on the further shore of what is to be known.
That is the principle of the three natures of non-existence; it is also not something to which sentient beings can easily approach,
because this principle is not the domain of practice for ordinary worldlings or those of the two vehicles.
Therefore, it is called "able to abide in harsh speech.
Furthermore, according to the esoteric terminology,
*pāruṣya* is named for abiding on the other shore (*pāra*).
This expresses the explicit meaning through esoteric terminology.
The treatise asks:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to speak words that are inconsistent [with conventional reality]?
"If a bodhisattva can analyze and break down all phenomena,
understanding them according to their respective categories.
The commentary explains:
The Bodhisattva is able to analyze and deconstruct all phenomena,
realizing that the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness are all non-existent.
This non-existence is not necessarily an absolute nothingness.
Nor is it definitively existent,
for both existence and non-existence are unapprehendable;
thus it is called speech that is inconsistent with what is expressed.
The Treatise says:

How does a bodhisattva practice *abhiṣekalābha* (the attainment of consecration)? It means that the bodhisattva repeatedly causes his own self to attain the unsurpassed meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
The Commentary says:
If taken in its direct sense,
*abhidhyā* (阿毘持訶樓) is a designation for covetousness; thus,
one who practices covetousness is so called.
One must necessarily delight in external objects; however,
because a bodhisattva constantly delights in causing his own body to attain the most excellent meditative concentration,
this is called "practicing desire."
Furthermore, if one relies on the esoteric terminology,
the term *abhiṣekaloka* (or *abhiṣekāloka*) signifies repeatedly attaining meditative concentration; thus,
by means of the esoteric terminology, the direct meaning is revealed.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva give rise to a mind of malice and harm?
It is when a bodhisattva, within the mental ground of both self and others, is able to destroy all afflictions.
The commentary states:
Hatred has the characteristic of malice and harm;
this is what the bodhisattva brings to mind.
Because one desires to sever all afflictions of oneself and others,
it is called "arousing a mind of malice and harm.
The treatise says:
How does a bodhisattva give rise to wrong views?
If a bodhisattva correctly observes the nature of pervasiveness of error in all places.
Commentary:
In the Mahāyāna, conceptual discrimination is considered a false nature.
Since the nature of conceptualization is omnipresent,
it constitutes a false nature within the dependent nature.
If one is free from conceptual discrimination,
this is called the true nature of the emptiness of persons and phenomena;
whereas the Hīnayāna regards the view of a self-identity as a false nature.
Therefore, because the view of a self gives rise to all afflictions,
if one is free from the view of a self,
no false attachments whatsoever can arise.
Having realized the true nature of the emptiness of persons,
the bodhisattva is able to observe this false nature in accordance with reality.
Because one perceives this as being wrong,
it is called the arising of false view.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter on the Seven Kinds of Wrong Views: Regarding wrong views, there are seven kinds.
The first is the wrong view of other vehicles.
Those who follow the right path yet separately seek parinirvāṇa without remainder are the śrāvakas who are ignorant of the Dharma.
Second is the view of false discrimination;
third is the view of clinging to precepts as purification,
which refers to various forms of divination regarding auspiciousness and misfortune.
These are false views, such as the view of bad precepts and so forth;
these constitute the view of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). As for the "view of bad precepts": [it refers to]...
Because they grasp at their own views,
these four consider themselves to possess right view,
though they are actually harboring deluded views.
This refers to the view that [the self] is identical to the mind, which is among the various views such as the afflictions.
Fifth is the view of concealment;
sixth is the view of feigning what is unreal.
"Concealment" means to use internal hiding as the primary aim;
"falsely manifesting what is unreal" refers to this.
Using external characteristics as being correct;
and seventh, impure views,
such as taking the mundane world to be nirvana, and so forth.
None of these views are permitted by the Buddha to be correct; therefore, they are called wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This principle applies within both the Three Vehicles and the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
The division [of the teachings] is designated by the term "One Vehicle" (ekayāna);
thus, it belongs to the One Vehicle.
Other meanings are as explained in a separate chapter.
Chapter on the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action: Regarding the ten wholesome actions, they are formed by reversing the preceding ten unwholesome actions to become the ten wholesome ones.
The meanings of "wholesome" (śubha) differ [according to context].
There are five kinds:
first, the ten wholesome actions of humans and devas;
second, the ten wholesome actions of śrāvakas.
Third, the ten wholesome actions of the pratyekabuddhas;
fourth, the ten wholesome actions of the bodhisattvas;
fifth, the ten wholesome actions of the buddhas.
Question: Since there are ten wholesome actions and five categories, the ten unwholesome actions should likewise correspond to those ten wholesome ones.
Answer: This is because the meaning of "wholesome" accords with principle.
Because the principle of the Dharma is profoundly deep, there are five stages.
This is not because of unequal evil karma;
rather, it is because various volitions arise from the differentiation of coarse characteristics within the unwholesome.
There is only one kind;
there are no five distinct levels.
These are the ten wholesome courses of action.
Through the wisdom of contemplation,
as wisdom gradually deepens,
merit likewise becomes increasingly subtle.
Therefore, they are not the same. Other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Regarding the four inversions clarified within the section on the precept of protecting living beings (*saṃgraha-śīla*): as for these four inversions—
The four are permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These two inversions are called "evil intentions" because they consist of focused mental application.
The two inversions are called "evil minds" because they are not practices of focused mindfulness; that is to say,
they consist of the thoughts of self and purity.
The second type of perverse intention is that of one who is single-mindedly devoted to practice;
it is the mind that seeks conditions for names and constantly delights in the two perversions.
It is called "mind" (*manas*) because it arises in dependence upon conditions.
That which contravenes reason is called "evil";
this gives rise to afflictions.
That which arises through mental attention is called "the practice of focused mindfulness.
The two inversions and the evil mind are not focused mindfulness;
their fundamental origination is the meaning of that mind.
The two inversions of self and purity,
in relation to the preceding [inversions] of permanence and bliss,
are called "mind" because they are the fundamental originators [of afflictions].
I am the essence of permanence;
purity is the source of bliss.
These two natures are established.
"Not arising from mental attention" means it is not produced by focused mindfulness.
"Perversion" refers to the inversion of permanence, bliss, self, and purity into impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity.
These are called the eight inversions.
Śrāvakas eliminate four inversions;
Bodhisattvas eliminate all eight inversions.
This is stated according to the manifest active mind;
if one considers the residual habits,
there are four inversions and eight inversions.
These are all eliminated by the Bodhisattva.
According to the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-yāna),
the tenth stage eliminates the afflictions without distinguishing them from their habitual tendencies (vāsanā).
According to the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-deśanā),
the seeds of the manifest afflictions are suppressed prior to the stages,
while those of the seeds are extinguished at the first stage (prathamā-bhūmi).
From the tenth stage downward,
habitual tendencies are gradually extinguished;
at the stage of Buddhahood, they are permanently severed.
If one distinguishes the nature of the afflictions,
the four inversions such as the notion of permanence and so forth are afflictions abandoned through the Path of Seeing.
The four [aspects] beginning with impermanence are afflictions of the mind;
this is according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Those delusions are vast and inexhaustible;
yet, by being able to realize the gateway of Samantabhadra,
they are all severed at once.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.

Regarding the fourth dhyānas and eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) within the section on "Aversion" (*nirveda*) in the third bhūmi: concerning the meditative absorptions of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
That is to say: the worldly first dhyāna,
the second dhyāna,
and the third dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna,
the sphere of infinite space,
and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
such are the meditative concentrations and the formless attainments.
It should be analyzed in detail by way of four aspects:
namely, by way of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and by way of purification (*vyavadāna*).
Because of establishment and because of purification.
As for "defilement":
This refers to the four neutral roots:
first, craving; second, views; third, pride; and fourth, ignorance.
By means of these four afflictions, one’s mind is defiled.
Within the gates of all defiled dhyāna concentrations,
it causes all obscured-unspecified afflictions and secondary afflictions of the form and formless realms to grow and arise without interruption.
Why is this? Because of the existence of craving,
they are defiled by the taints of relishing the higher dhyānas.
Because of craving for the pleasure of pure meditative concentration,
and because of the presence of views,
one is defiled by the afflictions associated with viewing higher dhyānas.
Because, relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
one gives rise to views that speculate about the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) and so forth;
this occurs by virtue of the presence of conceit (*māna*).
Pride is defiled by the afflictions of the higher meditative absorptions,
because one gives rise to arrogance based on having attained superior concentration.
Due to ignorance,
those seeking liberation are defiled by the impurities associated with the higher dhyānas.
Because they have not thoroughly realized the true path,
they constantly give rise to doubt regarding the supreme realization.
Whether for the sake of liberation or non-liberation,
such afflictions constantly defile the mind.
It causes the two types of afflictions— those of the form and formless realms, and those that are gross or subtle—
to continue in a stream;
this is what is meant by "pure and white."
That is to say, the pure meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and formless attainments (ārūpya) are called "pure and white" because they are wholesome by nature.
Although this is worldly,
it is also called "pure" because it is free from the stains of entanglements.
Regarding establishment,
there are four kinds of establishment:
namely, establishment by way of branches, establishment by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), establishment by way of categories, and establishment by way of names and characteristics.
Regarding the meditative absorptions (dhyāna),
they possess four foundations;
regarding the formless attainments (ārūpya), [the same applies].
There are only three types of factors for the removal of branches.
Regarding the establishment of the branches:
it is said that the first dhyāna has five branches.
What are the five? First, vitarka;
second, vicāra; third, prīti; fourth, sukha; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā).
The second dhyāna has four factors.
What are the four?
First, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; and fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
The third dhyāna has five factors.
What are the five? First, equanimity;
second, mindfulness; third, clear comprehension; fourth, bliss; and fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors.
What are the four?
First, purity of equanimity;
second, purity of mindfulness.
Third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
Question: Dharmas are immeasurable.
Why are only vitarka and the others established as factors?
Answer: Because they are the factors of counteraction and because they are the factors of benefit.
Because these two are the factors of the intrinsic nature that serve as their basis,
and because these three types of factors are complete and require nothing further,
[they are established] within the first dhyāna.
Vitarka and vicāra are the two factors of counteraction;
they are able to sever vitarka and vicāra such as desire, ill-will, and harmfulness belonging to the desire realm.
Joy and bliss are the two factors of benefit.
Because, through the factors of vitarka and vicāra,
having overcome that which is to be remedied by its remedy,
one attains the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
One-pointedness of mind is the essential factor that serves as the basis for those two,
because vitarka and the other factors function by relying on the power of concentration.
In the second dhyāna, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is the factor of antidote,
because it serves as the remedy for discursive thought (*vitarka*).
Joy and bliss are the factors of benefit;
one-pointedness of mind is the factor of essential nature, which serves as the basis for those two.
The meaning is as previously explained.
Within the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension are the factors of antidote.
Because these three can counteract joy and pleasure,
pleasure is the limb of benefit;
[the fourth is] one-pointedness of mind.
This is the meaning of the factors of the essential nature that serve as the basis for those two,
as previously explained.
Within the fourth dhyāna, there is the purity of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness.
This is the factor of counteraction,
because by means of these two, one is able to counteract pleasure; thus,
there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
These are the factors of benefit.
One-pointedness of mind is the factor of essential nature, which serves as the basis for those two.
Among the formless realms,
no constituent factors are established,
because of the single-flavored nature of śamatha.
Regarding the establishment of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*):
it means that by means of these seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
one enters the first dhyāna.
In this manner, it extends even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What are the seven types of mental attention? They are: the mental attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
The mental application of resolute belief,
the mental application of detachment,
and the mental application of gathering joy.
The mental engagement of observation,
the mental engagement of the culmination of the means,
and the mental engagement of the fruit of the culmination of the means.
This detailed analysis is as found in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*,
in the section on the "Subsequent Yoga" (*uttara-yoga-sthāna*).
How does one enter the first dhyāna?
By means of seven types of mental attention;
that is, by means of mental attention belonging to the stage of meditative concentration,
because one perceives the defects and so forth within the desire realm.
Having thoroughly understood coarse characteristics,
these characteristics are absent within the first dhyāna.
This is called the characteristic of tranquility;
this is termed the mental attention that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra*).
Such is this mental attention.
It is interspersed with hearing and reflection;
from this point upward,
one transcends hearing and reflection.
One-pointedly cultivating the signs of coarseness and calmness as the object of focus,
one practices śamatha and vipaśyanā.
To repeatedly contemplate the characteristics of coarseness and tranquility as they were previously investigated is called "attention through resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
By cultivating this, [one attains the first dhyāna].
The attention that arises together with the path of initial abandonment is called the attention of seclusion.
Because by means of this, one is able to sever the superior-grade afflictions and is able to distance oneself from the corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
this practitioner—
Furthermore, having rejoiced in the superior bliss of seeing and the superior merit of abandonment,
one touches a small portion of the joy and bliss born of seclusion.
When one wishes to eliminate lethargy and drowsiness,
one cultivates pure and sublime mental attention to gladden the mind;
this is called the mental attention of "delighting in the practice" (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manaskāra*).
Thus, for one who practices correctly,
because they are sustained by the excellence of skillful means,
[the roots of goodness increase].
He causes the afflictions, entanglements, and stains bound to the fruit of desire no longer to manifest.
For this reason, he carefully examines whether those afflictions have been abandoned or not.
Furthermore, he applies his attention to observe the pure signs that accord with their arising.
This is called the attention of investigation.
In this way, the practitioner repeatedly investigates and cultivates the remedies.
In order that all afflictions of the desire realm may attain dissociation for even a brief moment,
there is this mental attention associated with the path of counteraction.
Because this is the final preparatory application for the first dhyāna,
it is called the "attention of the culmination of preparation.
Immediately following this, one realizes the fundamental state.
The attention that occurs simultaneously with the first dhyāna is called the "attention to the fruit of the culmination of the means.
Furthermore, it is by means of the "attention to the discernment of characteristics" (lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī manaskāra).
One generates the mind of aspiration and resolve in order to correctly understand that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be attained;
for the sake of abandoning and for the sake of attaining.
Through attention consisting of resolute belief,
one initiates the correct application of means for the sake of the object sought.
By means of the mental application of detachment (*prāvivekya-manasikāra*),
one abandons the superior-grade afflictions;
by means of the mental application of delight in cultivation (*ratisaṃgrāhaka-manasikāra*).
One abandons the medium-grade afflictions through the mental application of investigation and settles the mind upon that which has been realized.
One becomes free from overweening pride;
by means of the mental attention that brings skillful means to completion,
one abandons the inferior grade of afflictions.
Through the mental attention that is the fruit of the culmination of skillful means,
one experiences the fruit of the cultivation of those mental attentions previously practiced;
for example, as when one cultivates the seven mental attentions in order to realize and enter the first dhyāna concentration.
In this manner, it should be understood accordingly up to the point of entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, as for the coarse characteristic (*audārikalakṣaṇa*):
This refers to the aspect of coarseness regarding all lower stages,
from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness.
Briefly, there are two kinds:
first, because one dwells in heavy suffering and lacks tranquility;
second, because the formations of life are meager and one's lifespan is short.
The characteristic of tranquility refers to all the higher stages,
from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because it is contrary to coarse characteristics.
Regarding the establishment by category:
in the first dhyāna concentration.
It is endowed with three grades of cultivation, namely:
weak, medium, and superior, as in the case of the first dhyāna.
The same applies to the three grades of cultivation for the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments.
Due to cultivating the first dhyāna through the weak, medium,
and superior grades, three types of karmic fruition arise within that first dhyāna.
As in the case of the first dhyāna,
so it is with respect to the cultivation and the arising of the fruit in the remaining dhyānas.
The same applies to each of the three grades.
Regarding those born as the fruit of the three grades of cultivation within the dhyānas:
these are the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā devas.
These and other such points are explained at length as previously stated.
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
there are no distinct locations.
The reason why the distinction of producing fruit is not established is that,
in the formless realm,
there are no stable abodes such as palaces or dwellings.
No distinction is established regarding the production of results;
however, because one has cultivated the formless attainments through three grades,
when their maturation arises, [the distinction is made].
There are those that are high and those that are low;
there are those that are inferior and those that are superior.
When that maturation arises, [it is so].
There are those who are superior or inferior due to differences in lifespan and so forth;
there are those who are excellent or lowly.
Because there is a distinction between the defiled and the undefiled,
and between the predominant and the minor.
Regarding the establishment of names and signs:
this refers to the immeasurable names for the various distinctions of samādhi within the four dhyānas.
It is incalculable and inconceivable. Why is this?
Within the meditative concentrations subsumed under the first dhyāna,
there are the samādhis entered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained ultimate great majesty and power.
As for that samādhi,
even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not yet understand its name.
How could one possibly know their number,
much less enter into realization?
This is as described in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the samādhis.
Their number exceeds one hundred.
In this manner, various samādhis are taught in other Mahāyāna sūtras as well.
Their number is immeasurable;
as it is with the concentrations included within the first dhyāna,
so it is with the concentrations included within the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments.
All that has been thus explained is based upon the purity of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
This refers to the ultimate concentration within the first dhyāna,
up to the ultimate concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is called purification.
Regarding those who practice the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*),
and the ultimate concentrations (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*): it is because they desire to separately manifest superior qualities and attain mastery,
cultivating them equally until the concentration reaches its ultimate limit that they are capable of such attainment.
Question: Why is it that supramundane concentration (*lokottara-samādhi*) is not mentioned?
Answer: Because the mundane concentration (*laukika-samādhi*) cited here serves as proof for the three stages, as they are alike in being mundane.

Furthermore, it is asked: According to the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*), the five factors of the first dhyāna are established separately, with the sixth—the mind of silence—constituting the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Why is this not the same [as other systems]?
Answer: That which is elucidated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other such treatises constitutes the meaning of the initial teaching;
it is identical to that of the Hīnayāna.
The fundamental cause and the numerical emergence of the essence of meditative concentration are established;
now, the *Ratnavali Sutra* accords with the meaning of the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao).
The cultivation of clarity is complete according to its numerical basis;
because it is explained in terms of the established locations within the stages of concentration,
the two numbers differ.
These numbers apply generally to the three vehicles as well as to the form-heavens and so forth of the Hīnayāna.
If they are designated within the teachings of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna),
they then belong to the One Vehicle.
Furthermore, the concentration attained by external worldlings is defiled by such things as the conceit of "I am," whereas the concentration of the śrāvakas is [not].
I am defiled by the habitual attachment to phenomena and so forth;
at the initial stage, the supramundane mind is defiled by afflictions and the like.
It should be understood accordingly that while the final teaching (zhōngjiào) is defiled by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three afflictions and so forth,
the provisional vehicle of the sudden teaching (dùnjiào fāngbiànshèng) and the ultimate one vehicle (jìngjiù yīshèng) are pure and undefiled.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.

Regarding the chapter on the three sufferings and the eight sufferings: the three sufferings are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
"Suffering" refers to the essence of painful feeling;
"suffering" refers to external instruments of suffering; "destruction" refers to the conditions for suffering.
"Suffering due to change" refers to the essence of painful feeling.
The practitioner’s conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are called "formations" because they are impermanent, shifting, and non-abiding;
they are also the conditions for the experience of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Question: Is the nature of impermanent formations merely the meaning of impermanence?
Why is it called suffering?
The answer is that impermanence has two meanings:
first, the impermanence of its own essence.
Second, impermanence that cuts to the very core of one's being is called suffering (*duḥkha*).
Although the meaning of "suffering" is the same,
there is a distinction between them based on whether the phenomenon is coarse or subtle.
It may also not be distinguished. Why?
Because impermanence cuts one to the core.
Included within the contemplations:
slight contact results in great suffering.
As for the eight sufferings:
The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what is loved,
the suffering of encountering what is hated, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
The suffering of the five aggregates of clinging has two meanings:
first, it subsumes the preceding seven types of suffering and collectively designates them as the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Second, the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of all sufferings is called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
While the eight types of suffering differ according to their specific instances,
the essential nature of suffering does not differ from the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*).
Second, the purpose for which the teaching of suffering arose was to produce a sense of weary detachment in those who have newly entered the Dharma.
It would then be subsumed under suffering alone;
there would be no logical basis for it to enter into the Four Truths.
It is subsumed within the Truth of Suffering. Why?
Because the holy teaching arises so that one may attain the truths.
The meaning of the Noble Truth of Suffering,
and so forth, may likewise be understood by analogy.
This is how it is known.
Because the meaning of the Mahāyāna encompasses both the beginning and the end:
this suffering is a category of suffering for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
and for *śrāvakas*, it enters into the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
If one is at the stage of a bodhisattva,
the initial teaching that all is empty is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
To penetrate through to the five aggregates of clinging as empty and without arising—
this is the meaning of suffering.
If one refers to the Final Teaching (Jiao),
suffering is itself True Suchness (Tathatā), and thus all phenomena are likewise such.
If one refers to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The preceding meaning refers to what is designated as the One Vehicle (ekayāna);
it is also called the One Vehicle by virtue of the four meanings,
such as the category of suffering and so forth.
Entering into the subtle [realms] such as Indra’s and so forth,
one accomplishes the inexhaustible;
the remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
The Chapter on the Four Immeasurables. Regarding the four immeasurables:
first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; and fourth, equanimity.
They are called "immeasurable" because they take three objects as their conditions.
First, the object-condition of sentient beings;
second, the object-condition of dharmas;
third, the objectless condition.
Regarding the object of sentient beings:

it is so called because one arouses loving-kindness by taking sentient beings as the object. Regarding the object of phenomena: [it is so called because one arouses loving-kindness] by taking phenomena as the object.
Because one gives rise to loving-kindness by taking conditioned phenomena such as the aggregates as its object;
"objectless" refers to giving rise to loving-kindness by taking the selflessness of phenomena as its object.
The same applies to joyful relinquishment (*muditā-tyāga*).
This principle does not exist within the three vehicles or the Hīnayāna; there, it exists only as the object-condition of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*).
In the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), however, this meaning is fully complete.
Why is this? Because dependent origination is inexhaustible.
If one were to define its essence as the nature of wisdom belonging to the Hīnayāna and other such vehicles, [it would be incomplete].
The initial teaching takes subsequently attained wisdom as its essence;
the final teaching takes wisdom that accords with reality and accords with the measure [of phenomena] as its essence. Why is this?
Non-conceptual wisdom is the essence of the bodhisattva; thus,
the meaning of the One Vehicle is inexhaustible.
Because the objects of knowledge are boundless,
they are called "immeasurable.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter on the Six Supernormal Powers: Regarding the six supernormal powers, they are:

first, the power of psychic transformation; second, the divine eye; third, the divine ear; fourth, knowledge of others' minds; fifth, recollection of past lives; and sixth, the exhaustion of outflows.
The bases of psychic power, the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of past lives—
these four are of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and are also said to be acquired at birth (*upapattilabdha*).

The supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds has as its nature the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds.
The supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
If it is that which is attained by one whose outflows are exhausted,
its nature consists of ten knowledges;
if it is the knowledge of another's exhaustion of outflows, [it consists of nine knowledges].
It has six types of knowledge as its nature, namely:
dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of exhaustion, knowledge of non-arising, knowledge of cessation, and conventional knowledge.
It is called a "supernormal power" (abhijñā) because it is unobstructed.
The knowledge of past lives and the divine eye are clear insights, not mere manifestations;
so too are the supernormal powers and the knowledge of others' minds.
This is a manifestation, not a clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) is both a clear knowledge and a manifestation.
The supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*) is neither a clear knowledge nor a manifestation.
Question: Why is it that among the fruits of the stages (*bhūmi*), the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are distinguished while the sixth supernormal power is not?
Answer: Because the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) that accomplish the supernormal powers belong to the mundane realm (*laukika*) and are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
If ordinary beings attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
the noble ones of the Hīnayāna attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Regarding the initial teaching, the essential nature [of these powers] is the same as that of the Śrāvakas.
It remains as suchness-wisdom;
its essence is emptiness.
In the Final Teaching, it is precisely suchness.
The sudden teaching is also the same.
As for the various meanings presented above,
they serve as designations for the One Vehicle.
This is precisely the One Vehicle.
If based on the Separate Teaching,
there are ten penetrations.
As explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokātītapaṭala*), the remaining meanings are as discussed in other chapters.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Thirty-two Marks" in the Fourth Ground: the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) are as follows.
1. The soles of his feet are level and even; 2.
the soles of his feet are marked with wheels having a thousand spokes;
3. his heels are broad and well-rounded.
Fourth, the bones of the ankles do not protrude.
Fifth, the calves are like those of the king of the eneya deer.
Sixth, the male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse king.
Seventh, his fingers are slender and long.
Eighth, with his hands standing flat, they reach his knees.
Ninth, his arms and elbows are well-rounded and muscular.
10. His hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes.
11. His hands and feet are soft and supple.
12. Seven parts of his body—the two hands, the two feet, the two shoulders, and the nape of the neck—are well-rounded and full.
Thirteen: his body is as perfectly proportioned as a nyagrodha tree.
Fourteen: according to the Mahāśāstra, the bodhisattva’s body is symmetrical;
the four sides are equal in measure, the body is smooth and straight, and the upper body is like that of a lion.
Fifteenth, his body is golden in color.
Sixteenth, his collarbones are filled out.
Seventeenth, his skin is fine and soft.
Eighteen: He is unstained by the eighteen impurities.
Nineteen: The hairs of his body point upward.
Twenty: Each hair curls to the right.
Twenty-first: the halo extends one fathom.
Twenty-second: above the throat, there are eleven marks;
first, forty teeth.
Second, his teeth are even and closely set.
Third, his teeth are white and pure.
Fourth, he has a broad and long tongue.
Fifth, his tongue obtains the supreme flavor;
sixth, he possesses the Brahma-voice;
seventh, the area of his cheeks is like that of a lion.
Eighth, his eyes are deep blue.
Ninth, his upper and lower eyelids blink like those of a bull king.
Tenth, there is a white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
Eleventh, the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
These thirty-two marks are obtained through no cause other than the practice of ethical discipline.
Why is this? Because one who violates the precepts shall not obtain even the body of a lowly human being.
How much more so regarding the marks of a Great Man;
furthermore, this is due to other causes,
as explained in the *Gopikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The thirty-two marks apply universally to ordinary beings, the Small Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the One Vehicle;
they differ only in their depth and shallowness.
Ordinary beings possess a person;
those of the Lesser Vehicle lack a person;
in the initial teaching, all is emptiness.
The Final Teaching is suchness;
it is the inexhaustible One Vehicle,
fully possessing the Indra-net and the subtle [jewel-adorned worlds], and so forth.
According to the distinct teaching,
its characteristics are like those of the atoms within ten lotus-treasury adorned world-oceans;
the remaining meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.
Chapter on the Eighty Minor Marks: Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), there are twenty [features] consisting of the nails and fingers of the hands and feet;
and eight locations on the hands and feet, both on the surfaces and the undersides, which are flat and full.

The two ankles, the two calves, the two knees, the two thighs, the two hips, the skin and organs, the two buttocks, the two flanks, the two armpits, the two breasts, the two shoulders, the two elbows, the two wrists, the waist, the back, the heart, the navel, the throat, and the abdomen.
All are exquisitely beautiful;
these are called the sixty secondary marks below the throat.
As for the term "thighs" (ūru):
Externally, these are called the thighs;
internally, they are called the hips.
Furthermore, there are the upper and lower teeth, the two lips, the two cheeks, the two temples, the two eyes, the two ears, the two eyebrows, the two nostrils, and the two corners of the forehead.
These are called the twenty minor marks above the throat.
The accumulation of merit of all sentient beings is equal to one of these hair-like marks, and [the merit of] all such hair-like marks [is equal to one major mark].
The accumulation of merit equal to one secondary mark (anuvyañjana) equals all the secondary marks.
When the accumulation of merit increases a hundredfold,
it equals one primary mark (lakṣaṇa), excluding the [final] mark.
When all other marks increase a thousandfold beyond the white tuft and the uṣṇīṣa,
one then attains the mark of the white tuft;
this constitutes the twenty-ninth mark.
It is called the mark of all marks.
The merit of the white tuft mark increases a hundred-thousandfold;
even up to the crown-protrusion and the invisible-crest mark, the merit of the white tuft mark increases to a billion-hundred-thousandfold.
He thus attains the mark of the Tathāgata’s conch-like voice;
the Tathāgata emits sounds at will with a pure Brahma-voice,
reaching even the Bodhisattvas of the stage of spiritual lineage throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions.
The seeds for the marks and signs of excellence are formed;
the Bodhisattva on the stage of practice through understanding cultivates and accumulates skillful means.
Bodhisattvas on the Ground of Pure Mind realize it;
for bodhisattvas on the remaining grounds,
it becomes progressively more purified.
The Tathāgata is ultimately swift and pure;
that which is not possessed by unsurpassed humans is partially possessed by the devas.
The Hīnayāna truly possesses [these qualities];
the Initial Teaching is emptiness, the Final Teaching is suchness,
and the One Vehicle is immeasurable.
Because it possesses the subtle qualities of Indra and so forth.
Other meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.
Regarding the "Seven Purifications" in the fifth chapter on the Seven Purifications within the Fifth Ground: as for these seven purifications—
First, purity of precepts; second, purity of concentration; third, purity of view; fourth, purity through overcoming doubt; fifth, purity regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
These five are designated by the same names in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
The latter two differ from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
These latter two are:
first, the purity of practice; second, the purity of the abandonment of practice.
Because the tenets of that [other] school have ceased,
it subsequently explains the purity of the abandonment of formations.
As for the name "Mahāyāna":
First is the severance of conduct;
second is the progressive purification of the factors conducive to enlightenment through reflection.
Based on this school, one gives rise to a superior and excellent aspiration by means of that severance of conduct.
Regarding the stage of the basis:
if according to the Hīnayāna,
it is prior to the path of seeing, consisting of ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
Next are three [moments] of the path of seeing;
next, one of the path of cultivation;
and next, one of the path of no-more-learning.
Regarding the Mahāyāna Treatise on the Three Stages (*Mahāyāna-tri-bhūmi-śāstra*):
the stages of "abandoning through practice" (*pratipakṣa-prahāṇa*) and "dwelling in practice" (*pratipatti-sthiti*) pertain to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
All other points are identical to those previously stated.
"Purity" (viśuddhi) is so named because it is distinguished by its excellence and freedom from defilement;
this meaning applies to all three vehicles as well as the Hīnayāna.
If it is intended specifically for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), [it refers to...]
This belongs to the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
There are ten kinds of purity of the One Vehicle,
as explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (Lokottaraparivarta).
The reason ten are mentioned is to manifest their immeasurability;
other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Chapter Ten: The Ten Truths. Regarding the ten truths:
it is that the bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, this noble truth of suffering, this noble truth of the origin of suffering, and this noble truth of the cessation of suffering;
and he knows, as they truly are, this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
This bodhisattva skillfully knows the conventional truth,
skillfully knows the ultimate truth,
skillfully knows the truth of characteristics, and skillfully knows the truth of distinctions.
He is skilled in knowing the truth of exposition;
he is skilled in knowing the truth of phenomena;
he is skilled in knowing the truth of arising; and he is skilled in knowing the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
They skillfully know the truth of the wisdom that causes entry into the path;
they skillfully know the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages;
and they skillfully know the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Because this bodhisattva, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings,
causes them to rejoice,
they skillfully understand conventional truth.
Because they have thoroughly penetrated the single characteristic of all phenomena,
they skillfully know the ultimate truth;
because they have awakened to the specific and general characteristics of phenomena.
One thoroughly knows the truth of characteristics because of awakening to the distinctions among phenomena;
one thoroughly knows the truth of distinctions.
Because one awakens to the discrimination of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana);
because one skillfully knows how to explain the establishment of the truths;
and because one awakens to the suffering and affliction of body and mind.
He skillfully knows the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*),
because he awakens to the continuity of the arising of all paths.
He skillfully knows the truth of birth (*jāti-satya*).
Because it ultimately extinguishes all feverish afflictions;
because it well understands the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, giving rise to non-dual practice;
and because it well understands the truth of the knowledge that leads one into the Path.
Because he has perfectly awakened to the characteristics of all phenomena,
he thoroughly understands the truth of the successive accomplishment of all bodhisattva stages,
as well as the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
This is known through the power of faith and understanding, not through the knowledge of ultimate omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Question: Do these ten truths apply to all three vehicles?
Answer: The ten truths of the Avataṃsaka are precisely the ten truths of the *Yingluo* (Adornment) of the One Vehicle;
these are identical to those of the Three Vehicles.
Why is this? Because it follows the fixed teaching.
The remaining meanings are explained extensively in the commentaries and treatises.
Chapter Six: Dependent Origination in the Sixth Ground. Regarding dependent origination, it is briefly explained by way of ten gates, namely:
the sequence of the causal factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Because they are subsumed within a single mind,
because they are accomplished through one's own karma,
and because they are inseparable from one another.
Because the three paths are uninterrupted;
because one contemplates the prior and posterior limits;
and because the three types of suffering accumulate.
Because they arise through causes and conditions;
because they are bound by the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions;
and because they accord with the contemplation of their exhaustion.
These ten cycles of the twelve links of dependent origination are subsumed within the meaning of the One Vehicle;
they constitute the ten cycles of dependent origination of the *Ābharaṇa* (The Ornament).
It is subsumed within the meaning of the Three Vehicles. Why is this?
Because they differ according to the distinctions in their respective teachings.
The remaining meanings are explained in the commentaries and separate chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on the Three Gates of Emptiness: this chapter is also called the Chapter on the Three Samādhis. The three gates of emptiness are:
first, emptiness (śūnyatā); second, signlessness (animitta); and third, wishlessness (apraṇihita).
Based on the object as the gateway,
and based on the observing wisdom,
these constitute the three samādhis.
This meaning applies to all three vehicles as well as the Hīnayāna.
If it is designated by the teaching of the One Vehicle,
then one enters the One Vehicle.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.

Regarding the Chapter on the Samādhi of Repeated Emptiness (*punar-śūnyatā-samādhi*): the samādhi of repeated emptiness refers to the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*).
The signless-signless samādhi and the wishless-wishless samādhi,
by means of the practice of impure emptiness.
To contemplate the untainted practice of emptiness is called the "emptiness of emptiness.
To contemplate the untainted practice of signlessness by means of the tainted practice of signlessness [is called the "signlessness of signlessness"].
It is called "the signless within the signless.
By means of the contaminated wishless practice,
one contemplates the uncontaminated wishless practice.
It is called "the wishless of the wishless.
This meaning belongs to the Hīnayāna;
if it is intended as a designation for the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), [it is understood differently].
If it refers to the One Vehicle, it belongs to the One Vehicle;
if it is designated as the Three Vehicles,
it belongs to the Three Vehicles.
The remainder is as explained in other chapters.

Regarding the chapter on the two emptinesses of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*): "the two emptinesses of person and phenomena" refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
The true suchness (tathatā) revealed by the absence of the grasping at a self of persons is called the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
The true suchness revealed by the absence of the grasping at a self of phenomena (dharma-ātman) is called the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
The emptiness of persons is common to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Yet it is not yet purified;
it becomes purified only upon reaching the Three Vehicles.
The emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) resides within the Three Vehicles.
Yet it is not yet purified;
it reaches ultimate purity through the One Vehicle.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter 74: The Four Schools of Thought on the Seventh Ground. Regarding the four schools of thought on the seventh ground:
first, the school of Prajñā;
second, the school of the Two Truths.
Third, the family of abandoning afflictions;
fourth, the family of purifying suffering.
These are comprised within the category of dwelling places.
It is called a "house.
A house refers to a dwelling.
Among the seven stages (bhūmis), it is thus designated.
Having accomplished the factors of the path for a long duration,
all obstacles are purified;
this is the final ultimate state of effortful signlessness.
Furthermore, it is able to accomplish the state of effortless signlessness;
therefore, it is called a "house" (*nāma*).
This meaning applies to the Three Vehicles.
If it is intended as a designation for the One Vehicle,
it then belongs to the One Vehicle;
this is the perspective of the Prajñā school.
It is the prajñā of true nature.
Regarding the term "truth" (satya):
it is called truth because its nature is real.
One who has abandoned the house of afflictions is intrinsically pure and free from afflictions.
Regarding the "purity of suffering":
the nature of suffering is emptiness;
this is called the purity of suffering.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Four Kinds of Non-arising Patience in the Eighth Ground": the four kinds of non-arising are, first, the non-arising of phenomena (*dharma-anutpāda*).
Second, the non-arising of intrinsic nature;
third, the non-arising of numerical distinctions;
fourth, the non-arising of distinctions in activity.
These four types of non-arising are explained in detail as in the treatise.
Regarding the non-arising of things (*vastu-anutpāda*):
Within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for the three vehicles,
because one understands phenomena as they truly are,
their intrinsic nature is non-arising.
Within the three vehicles,
the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) contemplates non-duality;
it is accomplished as perfectly equal and impartial.
Regarding the distinction of number:
in meaning, it refers to the differentiation of the boundaries of dharmic characteristics within the Three Vehicles;
that is, emptiness and non-differentiation.
Regarding the non-arising of distinctions in activity:
one shall achieve the perfection of Buddhahood within the Three Vehicles,
just as the celestial drum accomplishes its purpose without thought.
Ultimate non-conceptuality is established by relying on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
As for the meaning of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*),
it is established as the practice of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) through seeing and hearing at the final moment of the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-bhūmi*).
At the final stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one advances toward the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) and attains ultimate realization.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Chapter on the Three Worlds: Regarding the three worlds,
within the pure Buddha-lands there are three kinds of sovereign conduct.
1. Sovereign activity regarding the vessel world;
2. Sovereign activity regarding the world of sentient beings;
3. Sovereign activity regarding the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom.
Regarding those who exercise mastery over the receptacle world,
there are five kinds of mastery:
first, acting according to one's will.
First, he is able to manifest or not manifest;
second, whichever of these two he desires, he is able to manifest it;
third, whenever he desires it, he manifests it immediately.
Fourth, they can manifest according to the desired width or narrowness;
fifth, they can manifest according to the extent desired by the mind.
This is called mastery over the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
What is the sovereign practice regarding the world of sentient beings?
It is when this bodhisattva acts in accordance with the diverse faiths of sentient beings and in accordance with the distinctions of their resolute faith.
Within each and every Buddha-field,
and within each and every great assembly,
he manifests his own body in such and such a manner.
This bodhisattva,
if among a community of śramaṇas,
manifests the physical appearance and form of a śramaṇa.
In such various lands as these,
he manifests such diverse forms of himself.
What is the sovereign practice of the wisdom of perfect enlightenment?
The wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the wisdom of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), etc.
The Sūtra says:
"This bodhisattva remains far removed from all conceptualization regarding the marks of the body."
He attains equality of body.
This bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings and knows the bodies of buddha-fields.
He knows the body of karmic retribution;
he knows the body of a śrāvaka;
he knows the body of a pratyekabuddha.
He knows the body of the bodhisattva;
he knows the body of the Tathāgata;
he knows the body of wisdom.
One who knows the Dharma-body and knows the space-body is a bodhisattva.
Thus knowing the profound minds of sentient beings and giving rise to faith and joy,
one may take the bodies of sentient beings as one's own body,
or take one's own body as the bodies of sentient beings.
In this way, through these nine bodies,
the bodhisattva thus knows how to give rise to faith and joy within the deep minds of sentient beings.
It is accomplished through successive stages with sovereign mastery,
as explained in detail in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
This meaning is perceived and heard within the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, the Lesser Vehicle, and among humans and devas.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on the Ten Sovereign Powers: the ten sovereign powers are, first, mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*).
First, mastery over life, because one sustains a lifespan for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas.
Second, mastery over the mind,
because one enters into immeasurable asaṃkhyeya samādhis with wisdom.
Third, one attains mastery over objects,
because one manifests the maintenance and adornment of all worlds with immeasurable ornaments.
Fourth, one attains mastery over karma.
Fifth, they attain mastery over birth, because they manifest the abiding and sustaining of karmic retribution throughout the present, future, and past lives.
Sixth, he attains mastery over vows, because he manifests the arising of all worlds according to his heart's desire regarding the Buddha-fields and times.
Because he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi).
Seventh, he attains mastery over faith and understanding,
because he manifests the appearance of Buddhas filling all worlds.
Eighth is the mastery of obtaining as one wishes,
because one manifests miraculous transformations at will throughout all Buddha-lands.
Ninth, because of the clear manifestation of the dharma-gate of attaining mastery over phenomena that is boundless and without center;

tenth, because of the manifestation of the three types of awakening, adorned with the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities, and marks and signs of a Tathāgata, thereby attaining mastery over wisdom.
This meaning pertains to the qualities of fruition;
it is employed to manifest the sense of mastery in the eighth stage.
This meaning is common to all three vehicles.
The One Vehicle alone is ultimate. Why?
Because it is sovereign and boundless.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on the Ten Fears: the ten fears are, first, the fear of death.
Second, the fear of the defilements of affliction;
third, the fear of poverty;
fourth, the fear of evil karma.
1. Fear of the five evil destinies;
2. Fear of not obtaining what one seeks;
3. Fear of the karmic retribution for slandering the Dharma.
8. The fear of being unable to maintain one's livelihood when seeking a means of subsistence;
9. The fear of doubt as to how things might be;
10. The fear of the majestic power of the great assembly.
These ten types of fear are similar to those abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
While the five fears were already severed at the first stage,
these [ten] are now cited specifically to manifest the true Dharma (*saddharma*) of the eighth stage.
It is not meant that the eighth stage possesses such fears;
other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Chapter 91: The Ninth Stage, Section Eleven on the Meaning of the Eleven Dense Forests. Regarding the eleven dense forests:
First, the dense forest of the mental activities of sentient beings;
second, the dense forest of the activities of afflictions;
third, the dense forest of the activities of karma.
4. The thicket of conduct regarding the four faculties;
5. The thicket of conduct regarding faith;
6. The thicket of conduct regarding one’s nature.
7. The dense forest of the practices of the profound mind;
8. The dense forest of the practices of the latent tendencies;
9. The dense forest of the practices of birth.
10. The dense forest of the ten habitual tendencies;
11. The dense forest of the distinctions among the three groups.
The first phrase is a general summary.
The remaining ten phrases are distinct.
As for why the first phrase is "mental activity" (*cittacaryā*):
"mind" (*citta*) signifies manifoldness.
The remaining ten are simply the various meanings and characteristics of the mind, with no further distinction. Why is this?
Because they possess the meaning of the six aspects.
This meaning is because it is seen and heard by those of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, the Small Vehicle, and humans and devas.
Other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Eighty-Four Thousand Dharma Gates": as for the "eighty-four thousand," [it refers to] the eighty-four thousand [afflictions].
According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*,
when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment,
there were three hundred and fifty meritorious perfections (*pāramitā*).
From the first stage of the infinite Radiance (Prabhāketu) up to the stage of Distributing the Relics (Śarīrapratiṣṭhāpana),
one mounts these by means of the vehicle of the six pāramitās.
This constitutes two thousand one hundred degrees.
Multiplying this by the four great elements, the six bases of decay, and the ten dharmas,
it results in twenty-one thousand.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
it is also possible to take the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the Four Noble Truths as the vehicle; that is,
to take greed, hatred, delusion, and the four factors of equal proportion (*sama-bhāga*) as the vehicle.
This results in eighty-four thousand [teachings].
Such is the manner of the great number.
Within this, there are the factors of practice, faculties, desires, natures, diseases, and so forth.
Know it by analogy with this:
whether it be the Small Vehicle’s accordance with reality according to its gateways,
or the initial teaching of the Three Vehicles.
Its meaning is emptiness;
if according to the Final Teaching,
its meaning is suchness.
If one relies on the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
that which is referred to belongs to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
If one enters through the ten gates:
This belongs to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
Other meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.

Regarding the "Dense Forest of the Practice of Afflictions" (*kleśa-carita-gahana*) in the chapter on the practice of afflictions: the phrase "affliction-practice" (*kleśa-carita*) and so forth refers to... [text continues].
The One Vehicle is briefly divided into two meanings:
first, revealing afflictions by way of stages;
second, revealing afflictions according to their functional significance.
These two meanings are elucidated in relation to the Three Vehicles;
other schools may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the classification by stages:
this refers to how, within various teachings, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are used to clarify the boundaries for the abandonment of coarse and subtle [afflictions].
This belongs to the category of the Final Teaching (zhōngjiào),
as seen in the passage concerning the third stage in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages):
"All bonds of desire become further attenuated."
All fetters of form, all fetters of existence, and all fetters of ignorance have become entirely attenuated;
as for the fetters of views—
It has already been severed previously.
The commentary explains:
"All bonds of desire become even more attenuated."
Because all afflictions of the desire, form, and formless realms that are abandoned through the path of cultivation,
as well as their causes— the habitual tendencies of ignorance— are all rendered subtle and attenuated, and thus completely removed.
As for those bound by various views,
these have already been abandoned at the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) of the first stage (bhūmi);
thus, they appear only in the sūtras and śāstras.
The distinctions regarding the differences in severing delusions and their coarseness or subtlety— based on the stages of seeing and cultivation, as well as the nine or eleven stages and so forth—
are all subsumed under the Initial Teaching (Āgama).
As determined in the ten-fascicle *Śataśāstra*,
the conceptualized view of self (*parikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
while the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
the transformation of the defiled manas results in the attainment of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
At the time of initial clear observation (*abhisamaya*),
it has already been realized;
during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it becomes further purified.
Passages such as these all belong to the category of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).
As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "Innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)."
This uses afflictions as a metaphor to illustrate the paths of seeing and meditation,
just as there are three types of affliction— like skin, flesh, and heart.
During the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one abandons the "skin."
The two instances regarding the prohibition of meat during the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are similar in their meaning and application.
This applies whenever it occurs in the sūtras or śāstras.
Regarding the manifestation of specific ignorance based on the ten stages,
without distinguishing between coarse and subtle,
examples include the eleven types of ignorance and the twenty-two types of ignorance, and so forth.
All of these are subsumed under the teaching of direct progression within the initial teachings. Why is this?
Because it accords with the sudden severance of all afflictions at the final moment of mind in the tenth stage.
Second, regarding the manifestation of afflictions based on their functional meaning:
there are broadly two gates to the afflictions.
The first is the gate of differing from the Hīnayāna.
Second is the section on commonality with the Hīnayāna.
Regarding this commonality with the Hīnayāna,
it is further divided into two parts.
First is great delusion (*mahā-kleśa*).
That which possesses the five meanings of fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), impurities (*mala*),
and entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) is called great delusion.
The fetters are nine: first, the fetter of craving;

second, the fetter of aversion; third, the fetter of conceit; fourth, the fetter of ignorance; fifth, the fetter of views; sixth, the fetter of grasping; seventh, the fetter of doubt; eighth, the fetter of envy; and ninth, the fetter of avarice.
The meaning of "difficult to understand" is the meaning of "fetter.
Furthermore, there are five fetters:
namely, the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
Greed for the three realms constitutes the fetter of craving;
pride regarding the three realms constitutes the fetter of pride;
as for the remaining three, their meaning is that they are bound exclusively to the desire realm.
This is the meaning of "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, there are five fetters,
namely the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*).
These are the fetter of craving, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of the view of a self-identity, the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the fetter of doubt.
The first two belong to the lower realm,
while the latter three belong to the lower classes of beings.
These are called the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
"Lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
"lower class of beings" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, there are five fetters,
namely the five higher fetters:
the fetter of attachment to the realm of form, the fetter of attachment to the formless realm, the fetter of restlessness, the fetter of conceit, and the fetter of ignorance.
Greed abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the form realm is called "craving for form" (*rūpatṛṣṇā*);
craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*) is likewise.
So too are the restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms.
These constitute the three fetters.
These five can bind sentient beings so that they proceed toward the higher realms and do not follow toward the lower;
therefore, they are called "higher-tier" (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
Furthermore, this is the practice of the noble ones,
not the practice of ordinary people;
it is the practice of the noble ones among them, namely the *anāgāmins*.
They are called "higher" because they do not pertain to the two lower fruits.
Furthermore, there are four fetters:
the fetter of greed and envy, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of attachment to rules and observances, and the fetter of attachment to views.
Furthermore, there are three fetters, namely:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). The bonds consist of the four bonds.
1. The bodily bond of sensual desire;
2. The bodily bond of ill will; 3.
The bodily bond of attachment to precepts and observances.
The four types of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) constitute the bodily bond (*kāyabandhana*).
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), craving (*rāga*) is called the bond of craving (*rāgabandhana*),
and hatred (*dveṣa*) is called the bond of hatred (*dveṣabandhana*).
The grasping at precepts within the three realms is called the bond of grasping at precepts;
the grasping at views within the three realms is called the bond of grasping at views;
and the five aggregates are called the body.
These four must be accomplished through body and speech;
therefore, they are called "bodily bonds.
"Bond" (bandhana) carries the meaning of lack of autonomy.
Furthermore, there are three fetters:
namely, the fetter of greed, the fetter of hatred, and the fetter of delusion.
The messengers have four gateways.
First are the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):

namely, the latent tendency of sensual craving, the latent tendency of craving for existence, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of views, and the latent tendency of doubt.
Their meaning is that of following after and driving one along.
These are called the "proclivities" (anuśaya). There are ten proclivities: first, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
