second, the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi); third, false view (mithyādṛṣṭi); fourth, attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa); fifth, attachment to views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa); sixth, greed (rāga); seventh, hatred (pratigha); eighth, pride (māna); ninth, doubt (vicikitsā); and tenth, ignorance (avidyā).
Third, there are ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the thirty-six in the desire realm:
there are ten in the stage of suffering.
Below "origination" (samudaya) there are seven:
namely, wrong view, adherence to views, greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and ignorance.
Below "cessation" (nirodha) there are likewise seven.
As stated in the *Saṃyuktāgama*:
there are eight [afflictions] below the path, namely:
false view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and rituals, greed, hatred, pride, doubt, and ignorance.
There are four [fetters] to be abandoned through the path of cultivation:
namely, greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance.
Regarding the thirty-one [factors] of the form realm:
Below the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), there are nine;
excluding hatred (dveṣa), the rest are as explained for the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).
Below each of the Truths of Origination (samudaya) and Cessation (nirodha), there are six; below the Path (mārga), there are seven.
There are three types of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
all of which eliminate hatred (*dveṣa*).
The rest is as explained for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The thirty-one [factors] of the formless realm are as explained for the form realm.
There are four [categories], totaling one hundred and ninety-six latent proclivities (*anuśaya*).
There are one hundred and ninety-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This is because, among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, there is a distinction between those that are currently active (*samudācāra*) and those that are merely habitual (*vāsanā*);
thus, there are one hundred and ninety-six.
There are six defilements (*mala*):
namely, deceit, guile, pride, vexation, resentment, and malice.
Because they corrupt the mind, they are called "defilements."
There are ten *paryavasthānas* (entanglements):

namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), avarice (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), drowsiness (*middha*), anger (*krodha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
The term *paryavasthāna* means "to entangle," like a snare that binds and extensively ensnares.
This is the meaning of "envelopment" (paryavasthāna).
Furthermore, there are eight envelopments, namely: torpor (styāna).
Drowsiness, restlessness, remorse, envy, avarice, lack of shame, and lack of dread—
because these repeatedly increase and intensify,
binding and entangling the mind, they are called "envelopments" (paryavasthāna).
The five meanings of "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth explained above constitute the meaning of the great afflictions (*kleśa*);
those that do not possess these five meanings are not [so classified].
This is called a "minor affliction" (upakleśa).

Question: Since the meaning of a "proclivity" (anuśaya) is defined by possessing five characteristics, according to this definition of proclivity, it is that which is established [by the minor afflictions].
Question: For what reason is it said that the meaning of "proclivity" (anuśaya) enters into the five meanings [of the prefix *anu*], namely, the meaning of "being able to accomplish"?
Answer: The meaning of "proclivity" contains two senses.
First is the meaning of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*);
second is the meaning of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*). By virtue of the meaning of latent tendencies, one enters into the meaning of capability for accomplishment.
It is entered through the sense of "grossness" (*dausthulya*), which constitutes that which is to be accomplished.
Furthermore, it refers to the categories of the outflows of affliction (*kleśa*).
There are another twenty-nine gates.
First, the three outflows (*āsrava*):
namely, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
There are the outflows of the taints (āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava).
The afflictions (kleśa) of the desire realm, excluding ignorance, constitute the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava).
The afflictions of the higher realms, excluding ignorance, constitute the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava).
Ignorance within the three realms constitutes the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Because these three flow forth continuously and without interruption, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
Second, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
That is to say, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These four do not accord with correct principle;
they are termed "inversions."
The four floods (*ogha*) are:
the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
These are the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The afflictions of the lower realms, excluding views and ignorance, are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The afflictions of the higher realms,
excluding views and ignorance, are called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*).
The views within the three realms are called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*).
The ignorance within the three realms is called the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
These four are called floods (*ogha*) because they sweep away.
There are four types of clinging (*upādāna*):

namely, clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*).
The afflictions of the desire realm,
excluding the [wrong] views, are called "grasping at desire" (*kāma-upādāna*).
The four [wrong] views within the three realms are called "grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*).
The grasping for precepts and observances within the three realms is called "grasping at precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
The afflictions of the upper realms,
excluding views, are called "grasping at the doctrine of self" (ātmavādopādāna).
Because there is no self,
the mere grasping of these words is called "grasping at the discourse on self" (*ātmavādopādāna*);
it constitutes a fixed adherence that leads to harm.
This is the meaning of "clinging.
There are five hindrances:
namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
These five exist only in the desire realm;
because they can obscure the three trainings,
they are called hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Sensual desire and ill will can obscure the aggregate of ethical discipline;
restlessness and remorse can obscure the aggregate of meditative concentration.
Sleep can obscure the category of wisdom;
doubt can obscure three categories;
and the six and five views [obscure] five categories.

These are: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
They are called "views" because they possess four characteristics:
first, the capacity for observation; second, active engagement; third, firmness in their objects of apprehension; and fourth, intensity toward their conditions.
The seven types of stinginess (*mātsarya*) are set forth in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun):

namely, stinginess regarding one’s dwelling (*āvāsa-mātsarya*), stinginess regarding one’s family (*kula-mātsarya*), stinginess regarding offerings (*lābha-mātsarya*), stinginess regarding praise (*varṇa-mātsarya*), and stinginess regarding the Dharma (*dharma-mātsarya*).
Avarice is defined as the state of being miserly or withholding.
The eighth is the "five minds of resentment.
Resentment refers to doubting the Buddha, doubting the Dharma, doubting the Sangha, doubting the precepts, and doubting the teachings;
as well as harsh speech and slanderous judgment.
It ruins the mind and prevents the formation of roots of goodness; therefore,
it is called "mental obstruction."
The *Abhidharma* states that nine of the six [contacts] give rise to craving:
namely, craving arising from eye-contact,
and craving arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
The seventeen outflows:
namely, the outflows to be abandoned by seeing the truths and the outflows to be abandoned by cultivation.
The outflows abandoned through detachment,
the outflows abandoned through cultivation,
and the cessation abandoned through relinquishment.
The outflows to be abandoned by cultivation;
the outflows to be abandoned by suppression;
the eleven [categories] and the four yokes.
These are the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
The twelve [types of] pride consist of:
pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, the pride of "I am," overweening pride, the pride of inferiority, false pride, and haughty pride.
To think oneself superior to those who are inferior is called pride (*māna*);
to consider oneself equal to those who are equal is also called pride;
and to think oneself superior to those who are one's equals is called great pride (*adhimāna*).
To be haughty toward those who are superior is called *māna* (pride).
To [cling] to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
To say of one who is greatly superior that one is only slightly inferior is called *ūnamāna* (the pride of inferiority).
To be self-exalting despite lacking virtue is called false pride;
likewise, to exalt oneself by means of unwholesome dharmas is also called false pride.
[This occurs] toward virtuous persons and those who are venerable.
Refusing to pay homage is called arrogance.
Regarding the thirteen [categories] and the sixty-two views:
this refers to the arising of twelve views concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Permanent and impermanent;
both permanent and impermanent;
neither permanent nor impermanent.
Finite, infinite, both finite and infinite,
neither finite nor infinite.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
he has gone, or he has not gone,
or he has both gone and not gone.
It is neither going nor not going.
The aggregate of form has twelve phrases;
so too for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
There are also twelve [views],
totaling sixty;
adding the view that the body and the life-principle are distinct makes sixty-two.
One may also add the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, making fourteen types of discursive thought (vitarka). These eight types of discursive thought are:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of cruelty, thoughts of kin, thoughts of one's country, thoughts of immortality, thoughts of gain, and thoughts of disparaging others.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
the seventh is called the thought of contempt,
and the eighth is called the thought of noble lineage.
The fifteen hundred and eight afflictions refer to the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) plus their ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*);
these are called the one hundred and eight afflictions.
16. The three unwholesome roots, namely:
greed, hatred, and delusion.
17. The three stumps.
That is to say, greed, hatred,
and delusion. The eighteen threefold stains are greed, hatred, and delusion.
Nineteen: the three burnings and harms, namely greed, hatred, and delusion;
twenty-three: the arrows.
That is to say, greed, hatred, and delusion.
They exist in twenty-one [mental states].
That is to say, greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-two are unwholesome actions, namely:
greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-three are the deprivations.
That is to say, greed, hatred, and delusion.
The twenty-four [types of] threefold fevers refer to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-five: the three afflictions, namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-six: the three disputes.
That is to say: greed, hatred, and delusion.
The twenty-seventh [category], the three blazing fires, refers to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-eight are the thickets of entanglement (*trai-gahana*),
namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Twenty-nine are the obstructions (*trai-vighāta*).
That is to say: greed, hatred, and delusion.

Furthermore, these afflictive defilements consist of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), their objective conditions (*ālambana*), their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), their objects (*ālambanaviṣaya*), and their coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
It should be known that each has twenty kinds of characteristics.
Regarding the fact that there are twenty kinds of active afflictions:
First, the manifestation of entanglements according to one's desires,
which refers to householders;
second, the manifestation of entanglements not according to one's desires.
This refers to those who have gone forth.
There are three things they do not discern:
namely, those who dwell among those who preach the Dharma poorly.
Fourth, there is that which is discerned,
namely, those who have well expounded the Dharma.
Fifth, there is mutual predominance.
This refers to those whose conduct is dominated by greed and so forth;
for them, all six [factors] are equal.
This refers to those whose conduct consists of equal proportions.
Seventh, those with attenuated defilements,
namely those whose conduct is characterized by thin dust;
eighth, the manifestation of outward-directed fetters.
This refers to those who have attained permanent freedom from desire.
Nine types of internal-door entanglements manifest;
that is, for those who have attained freedom from desire by means of the mundane path.
Tenth, the manifestation of the fetter of excessive obsession,
which refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Eleventh, the manifestation of the fetter of loss of mindfulness.
This refers to those in training (śaikṣa) who manifest twelve types of entanglements (paryavasthāna),
namely those who are firmly attached.
Thirteen are the manifestations of innate fetters,
namely those who do not firmly adhere.
Fourteen are the manifestations of analytical investigation.
This refers to those who observe with joy.
Fifteen types of non-autonomous activity refer to those who are subject to sleep.
Sixteenth, the manifestation of mastery,
which refers to the awakened one.
Seventeenth, the manifestation of being beyond salvation.
This refers to those who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa;
eighteen [factors] are present in those who can be saved,
namely, those who possess the nature for parinirvāṇa.
19. Manifestation of grasping at signs (*nimittābhiniveśa-pravṛtti*):
that is, when one investigates and grasps the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in accordance with those dharmas.
20. Manifestation of non-grasping at signs (*animittānabhiniveśa-pravṛtti*).
This means not conceptualizing those [objects] in accordance with their phenomena and not grasping their characteristics.
Regarding the twenty kinds of conditions for afflictions:
First, pleasure;
second, suffering;
third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Fourth, desire;
fifth, vitarka;
sixth, contact.
Seventh, habitual practice in the past;
eighth, latent tendencies;
ninth, not associating with virtuous friends.
Tenth, not hearing the true Dharma;
eleventh, improper mental attention;
twelfth, lack of faith.
Thirteenth, laziness;
fourteenth, loss of mindfulness;
fifteenth, distraction.
16. Lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*).
17. The affliction of heedlessness (*pramāda-kleśa*).
18. The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
Nineteenth, through the departure from desire;
twentieth, through the afflictions arising from rebirth.
Thus, there are twenty kinds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
First, the proclivities of the non-concentrated stage;
second, the proclivities of the concentrated stage;
third, the proclivities that follow their own respective objects.
Fourth, latent dispositions that follow other objects;
fifth, impaired latent dispositions;
sixth, unimpaired latent dispositions.
7. Latencies that are concordant;
8. Latencies that are non-concordant;
9. Fully perfected latencies.
10. Deficient latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
11. Latent dispositions that can be destroyed.
12. Latent dispositions that cannot be destroyed.
Thirteen are the predominant latent tendencies;
fourteen are the equal latent tendencies;
fifteen are the subtle latent tendencies.
16. Latent dispositions accompanied by vitarka;
17. Latent dispositions without vitarka;
18. Latent dispositions that give rise to much suffering.
Nineteenth, the latent tendency toward suffering in those who have been born;
twentieth, the latent tendency toward suffering in those who have not been born.
These are the twenty kinds of objects upon which the afflictions take their support.
1. Taking an object that possesses substantial reality as its objective condition;
2. Taking an object devoid of substantial reality as its objective condition; 3.
Taking an object characterized by specific characteristics as its objective condition.
Fourth, those that take common characteristics as their object;
fifth, those that take directly perceived objects as their object;
sixth, those that take imperceptible objects as their object.
7. Those that take external objects as their domain;
8. Those that take internal objects as their domain;
9. Those that take the afflictions of their own category as their domain.
10. Taking other categories of afflictions as objects;
11. Taking one's own objects as objects; 12. Taking other objects as objects.
Thirteen take non-existent objects as their domain;
fourteen take contaminated objects as their domain;
fifteen take uncontaminated objects as their domain.
Sixteen take conditioned phenomena as their object;
seventeen take unconditioned phenomena as their object;
eighteen take the objects of one's own mental discrimination as their object.
Nineteenth, it takes the object of conceptualization through recollection as its condition.
Twentieth, it takes the object of phenomenal characteristics as its condition.
There are twenty types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
First, the heaviness of the nature of retribution;
second, the heaviness of the nature of afflictions;
third, the heaviness of the nature of karma.
1. The coarse heaviness of the four afflictive obscurations;
2. The coarse heaviness of the cognitive obscurations; 3.
The coarse heaviness of the obscurations to meditative concentration.
Seventh, the heavy burden of karmic obstructions;
eighth, the heavy burden of retributive obstructions;
ninth, the heavy burden of obstructions to the wholesome.
10. The heaviness of improper discursive thought;
11. The heaviness of sorrow and affliction;
12. The heaviness of fear.
Thirteen: the heavy burden of fatigue;
fourteen: the heavy burden of food;
sixteen: the heavy burden of sensual desire.
Seventeenth, the heavy burden of discordant elements;
eighteenth, the heavy burden of transformation over time;
nineteenth, the heavy burden of death.
Twenty: the pervasive grossness (*dausthulya*).
Furthermore, to explain briefly, the thorough knowledge of afflictions is by way of five aspects:

namely, the aspect of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of their cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of their categories (*prakāra-lakṣaṇa*), the aspect of mental distraction toward objects (*viṣaya-citta-vikṣepa-lakṣaṇa*), and the aspect of their fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
The above clarifies that the various *anuśayas* (proclivities), afflictions (*kleśa*), and so forth,
share the same names as those in the Hīnayāna, yet their meanings differ.
If one follows the Hīnayāna method...
That which is called "real" would then possess substantiality; however,
according to the initial teaching of the Mahāyāna, intrinsic nature is itself empty,
existing as nothing more than name and function.
These are called the proclivities (*anuśaya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the two distinct approaches from the perspective of the Hīnayāna, there are two gates.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is included solely within the gate of the stage of entry into the teaching for those who proceed directly.
First, ignorance regarding the nature of ordinary beings;
second, ignorance regarding the performance of improper conduct toward sentient beings based on karma and so forth.
Third, the ignorance of sluggishness of mind, which is the forgetfulness of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
fourth, the ignorance that arises together with the subtle afflictions and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
fifth, the ignorance regarding the parinirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle.
Sixth is the ignorance of coarse modes of activity;
seventh is the ignorance of subtle modes of activity;
eighth is the ignorance of mental application toward signs.
Ninth is the ignorance that lacks effort regarding the task of benefiting sentient beings;
tenth is the ignorance that lacks mastery over all phenomena.
Both are termed "ignorance" because the mind is deluded and lacks understanding.
The second [category] consists of twenty-two types of ignorance (*avidyā*):
first, the ignorance of conceptualizing a self in phenomena (*dharma-ātman-vikalpa-avidyā*);
second, the ignorance regarding karma leading to the evil realms (*durgati-karma-avidyā*).
Third, ignorance regarding subtle transgressions;
fourth, ignorance regarding the various characteristics of karmic formations;
fifth, ignorance regarding craving for sensual desire.
Sixth is the ignorance of the perfection of the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining;
seventh is the ignorance of craving for meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
eighth is the ignorance of craving for the practice of the Dharma.
Ninth is the ignorance of conceptualizing birth-and-death and nirvana as being exclusively opposed to one another;
tenth is the ignorance regarding the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) subsumed under skillful means;
eleventh is the ignorance regarding the arising and continuity of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
12. Ignorance arising from the conceptualization of the twelve marks;
13. Ignorance arising from the subtle movements of the marks;
14. Ignorance regarding the skillful means of one-pointed contemplation on the markless.
Fifteenth is the ignorance regarding the exertion of effort in the contemplation of the signless (*animitta*).
Sixteenth is the ignorance regarding mastery over the movement of signs (*nimitta*).

Seventeenth is the ignorance regarding the immeasurable dhāraṇīs of skillful speech that provide mastery over immeasurable correct teachings, immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables, and the ability to answer difficult questions.
18. Ignorance regarding the resolution of doubts and the generation of understanding based on the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
19. Ignorance regarding the wisdom of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
20. Ignorance regarding entry into the subtle and secret Buddha-dharmas.
21. Ignorance that consists of subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge;
22. Ignorance that consists of subtle obstruction toward all objects of knowledge.
These two gates of affliction are restricted to the direct-advancement gate within the initial teaching.
This is known because:

By means of these two gates, one should know that afflictions pervade all ten stages regardless of whether they are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), or coarse or subtle;
this accords with the principle that delusions are suddenly severed at the final moment of mind in each of the ten stages.
Furthermore, according to the Final Teaching (Jiaojiao),
there are sixteen gates of affliction (*kleśa*).
First, there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*).
That is to say, the afflictive hindrance and the cognitive hindrance;
furthermore, there are two types of ignorance,
namely the two hindrances of affliction and cognition.
There are three obstacles within the three realms of existence,
namely those of the skin, the flesh, and the heart;
these three obstacles are also called the skin, the flesh, and the bone.
There are four obstacles to the four states of existence:
namely, the obstacle of lack of faith in the icchantikas,
and the obstacle of the grasping at a self among the non-Buddhists.
The śrāvakas have the obstacle of fear toward suffering;
the pratyekabuddhas have the obstacle of relinquishing great compassion;
and there are the obstacles of the five states of existence and the six corruptions.
This refers to the specific obstacles eliminated by each of the six pāramitās.
There are eight types of false conceptualization (vikalpa):

namely, the conceptualization of recollection, the conceptualization of non-recollection, the conceptualization of both recollection and non-recollection, the conceptualization of self, the conceptualization of "mine," the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, the conceptualization of differentiation, and the conceptualization of grasping and accumulation.
The first three are afflictions of the skin;
the next two are afflictions of the flesh;
the next three are afflictions of the mind.
There are seven types of existence and nine afflictions, as stated in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*:

first, latent greed; second, latent anger; third, latent ignorance; fourth, the extremely heavy, manifest delusions of greed, anger, and ignorance; fifth, the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*); and sixth, those [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*).
The seventh is that which is abandoned through cultivation; the eighth is the afflictions of the impure stages; and the ninth is the afflictions of the pure stages.
The first four and the seventh are abandoned through cultivation and have the "outer-skin" afflictions as their essence.
The sixth consists of the fleshly afflictions (*māṃsa-kleśa*) eliminated by the vision of the truths;
the fifth is the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*);
and the eighth is the delusion of the impure stage (*aśuddha-bhūmi*).
The ninth, the ground of purity (*śuddhabhūmi*), takes the afflictions that bind the mind as its essence.
There are eight grounds of abiding afflictions (*vāsabhūmi-kleśa*):

namely, the ground of abiding in the view of a single location (*ekadeśa-dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*), the ground of abiding in desire-attachment (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*), the ground of abiding in form-attachment (*rūparāga-vāsabhūmi*), the ground of abiding in existence-attachment (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*), and the ground of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
The basis upon which all afflictions rely is called the "ground of abiding" (sthiti-bhūmi).
To perceive [them] as a single locus is the affliction of the flesh.
The three, beginning with desire-attachment,
are the superficial afflictions;
the ground where ignorance dwells is the fundamental.
This mind is afflicted by defilements.
Within the nine realms of existence, there are thirteen defilements, namely:
seven views and six attachments.
The seven views are: first, wrong view;

second, the view of self; third, the view of eternalism; fourth, the view of nihilism; fifth, the view of attachment to precepts and rituals; sixth, the view of attachment to fruits; and seventh, the view of doubt.
It is called "seeing" because it perceives all objects.
As for the six types of attachment:
first, greed; second, craving; third, anger; fourth, delusion; fifth, desire; and sixth, pride.
Within the dharma-realm,
all afflictions arise at all times,
with thirteen as their basis.
Ignorance acts as the basis for the thirteen [factors];
within the dharma-realm,
it separately brings about the retribution of the three realms.
Question: Since these thirteen afflictions lack the grasping for phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), why are they not included within the tenets shared with the Hīnayāna?
Answer: The intent of the sutra is to clarify that these thirteen delusions arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) and are capable of producing various karmas.
Because the station of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) within the desire realm is its cause,
it is not included among the shared [teachings] of the Hīnayāna.
There are eighteen inversions.
That is to say: permanence, bliss, self, and purity; impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.
These four inversions obstruct the śrāvakas;
these eight inversions obstruct the bodhisattvas.
Eleventh, there are four types of denial (*apavāda*):

Twelfth, there are five types of distraction (*vikṣepa*).
1. Distraction of intrinsic nature, which refers to the five sensory consciousnesses.
2. External distraction.
This refers to the mind racing toward external objects.
Third is internal distraction,
which refers to the mind’s fluctuation between elation and depression, as well as relishing [meditative experiences] and so forth.
Fourth is the distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*),
which refers to the reckoning of "I" and "mine," and so forth.
Fifth is the distraction of discursive thought (*vitarka*).
This refers to abandoning the Mahāyāna and contemplating the Hīnayāna;
regarding the first two [obstacles], it causes those not yet attained to remain unattained.
The third causes those who have already attained [the fruit] to fall away;
the fourth prevents them from attaining liberation;
the fifth prevents them from attaining unsurpassed bodhi.
Thirteenth, there are two types of afflictions:
namely, latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) and manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
Fourteenth, there are also three inversions:
namely, inversion of perception, inversion of view, and inversion of mind.
Fifteenth, there are twelve false conceptualizations.

Regarding the prātimokṣa:
That is the discipline of the seven classes of followers;
it consists in being able to practice the avoidance of misconduct and sensual conduct.

Upāsikā, you have undertaken the vows for as long as life lasts;

The *Upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts for day and night are established so that one may gradually train and study.
Question: Regarding the *śikṣāpada* of a single portion for an *upāsaka*, is it said that he fulfills them or does he not fulfill them?

"Can one achieve the status of an upāsaka precept-holder?

This means that when jealousy arises, one must sprinkle water to remove it; for half a month, all matters shall be as previously stated.

As in the preceding separate chapter,

Now, to briefly enumerate the categories of karma,
there are thirty-six types.
The first is "intentional" and "unintentional."
The second pair of karmas consists of intentional karma and non-intentional karma.
That which is performed with prior knowledge is called intentional karma.
To act without knowing is called non-intentional karma;
furthermore, according to the terminology of the supreme teaching, it is called intentional karma.
Karmas that do not reach the point of instruction are called non-intentional karmas.
There are two types of sinful karmas:
namely, light sinful karmas and heavy sinful karmas.
The three types of action for the benefit of self and others: namely,
action for great benefit, and action for small benefit.
The four types of merit and so forth are the three kinds of karma:
namely, meritorious karma, non-meritorious karma, and immovable karma.
The five are the three kinds of karma.
These refer to the three types of unwholesome conduct— bodily, verbal, and mental—
which are also termed wrong conduct.
These refer to misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
The sevenfold threefold sublime conduct is also called right conduct.
These are called excellent conduct of body, excellent conduct of speech, and excellent conduct of mind.
There are eight types of unskillful conduct:
namely, unskillful conduct of body, unskillful conduct of speech, and unskillful conduct of mind.
To act in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma and the Vinaya is called "lack of skillful means.
Ninth: the three types of skillful means practice.
This refers to the practice of skillfulness in body, skillfulness in speech, and skillfulness in mind.
There are thirteen types of wrongness:
namely, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
Arising from hatred and delusion,
the four verbal transgressions are called wrong speech;
they arise from hatred and delusion.
The three unwholesome actions of the body are called wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*);
they arise from the affliction of greed.
The unwholesomeness of body and speech is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The eleventh triad is the three right [paths]:
namely, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
These arise from non-hatred and non-delusion.
The four virtues of speech are called right speech;
they arise from non-anger and non-delusion.
The three virtues of body are called right action.
That which arises from non-attachment is called right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), being the virtue of body and speech.
It is termed "right" because it accords with principle.

The karma of the three periods of time refers to karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*), karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*).
It is called "karma of the three periods of time" because it is designated according to the time in which its results are received.
Thirteen are the karmas that yield three types of retribution:
namely, karma with pleasant retribution, karma with painful retribution, and karma with neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution.
Fourteen are the karmas bound to the three realms.
These are: karma bound to the desire realm, karma bound to the form realm, and karma bound to the formless realm;
and the three types of karma consisting of the fifteen crookednesses and so forth, namely:
crooked karma, defiled karma, and turbid karma.
Karma arising from flattery is called "crooked karma.
Karma arising from hatred is called "corrupt karma.
Karma arising from greed is called "turbid karma."
Sixteenth, the three natures of karma:
namely, wholesome karma,
unwholesome karma, and indeterminate karma.
Seventeenth are the three karmas of fulfillment (*pūrṇakarma*):
namely, bodily karma of fulfillment, vocal karma of fulfillment, and mental karma of fulfillment.
Because the bodily conduct of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is fully perfected, it is called "bodily fulfillment."
The same applies to speech and mind.
There are eighteen types of training in the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā-karma*), namely:
the karma of training (*śaikṣa-karma*), the karma beyond training (*aśaikṣa-karma*), and the karma that is neither of training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-karma*).
The untainted karma of those in training is called the karma of training;
the untainted karma of those beyond training is called the karma of no-more-training;
all tainted karma is [the remainder].
It is called karma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Nineteen are karmas of the three types of abandonment, namely:
karma abandoned by vision, karma abandoned by cultivation, and karma not to be abandoned.
Twenty-three are karmas:
namely, past karma, future karma, and present karma.
Twenty-one are obstacles.
These are the karmic obstruction, the afflictive obstruction, and the retributive obstruction.
There are twenty-two aspects of karma:
namely, black karma with black retribution, white karma with white retribution, black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution, and neither-black-nor-white karma that is without retribution.
Twenty-three or twenty-four precepts:
namely, the prātimokṣa precepts, the dhyāna-accompanied precepts, the path-accompanied precepts, and the abandonment precepts.
Twenty-four or twenty-five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
That is to say: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
The first two constitute a betrayal of those who have provided sustenance;
the latter three are called "heinous crimes" (*ānantarya*) because they destroy the field of merit.
Twenty-five: the five precepts, namely:
not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking intoxicants.
Restraining the body and speech is called *śīla* (precepts).
Twenty-six [types of conduct] constitute the five wrong modes of livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
First, for the sake of gain and offerings,
they falsely manifest wonders and marvels.
Second, for the sake of gain and offerings...
They speak of their own merits for three reasons: first, for the sake of gain and offerings; second, for the sake of gain and offerings;
and third, to practice divination of good and bad fortune.
Fourth, they preach to others for the sake of gain and offerings,
speaking in a loud voice and manifesting an air of authority.
5. To cause others to feel awe and reverence;
for the sake of gain and offerings, one proclaims the offerings one has received.
Because it agitates the human mind,
and because one sustains life through wrong causes and conditions, it is called "wrong livelihood.
[This concludes] the twenty-seventh [section], the six types of action.

That is to say: karma resulting in rebirth as a hell-being, karma resulting in rebirth as an animal, karma resulting in rebirth as a hungry ghost, karma resulting in rebirth as a human, karma resulting in rebirth as a deva, and karma with indefinite timing of retribution;
as well as the twenty-eight types of unwholesome restraint.
That is to say: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech.
In all these instances, one gives rise to unwholesome restraint.

namely, abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous speech.
Because one does not sever the roots of goodness at any time,
one generates the wholesome restraint (kuśala-saṃvara) through thirty-eight kinds of speech.
First, seeing something and saying one did not see it;
second, not seeing something and saying one saw it;
third, not seeing something yet claiming to have seen it.
When asked, he says he does not see;
yet when questioned regarding the four views,
he says that he sees them.
Fifth, seeing what one has seen;
sixth, not seeing what one has not seen;
seventh, claiming not to have seen what one has actually seen.
When asked, he said, "I did not see.
Regarding the eight instances of not seeing yet calling it seeing,
when questioned, he immediately said, "I saw."
The first four are impure speech;
the latter four are pure speech.
[These constitute] the thirty-one eightfold precepts.
The precepts for that very night are:
first, not to kill living beings;

And not eating past midday.

Regarding the thirty-two [factors], there are eight wrong paths (*mithyātva*), namely:

wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), wrong resolve (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*), wrong effort (*mithyāvīrya*), wrong mindfulness (*mithyāsmṛti*), wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*), wrong speech (*mithyāvāk*), wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*), and wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Third, there are thirty unwholesome courses of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), namely:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view.
That which violates reason and harms things is called unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The volition (*cetanā*) that binds [the mind] is called karma;
its course of action is called the path (*mārga*).
Thirty-four paths of wholesome action (*kuśala-karmapatha*), namely:

refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, refraining from divisive speech, refraining from harsh speech, refraining from frivolous speech, absence of ill will, absence of covetousness, and right view.
That which accords with principle and benefits sentient beings is called "wholesome.

There are four or three types of births.

There are four kinds of nutriment.
These are the four nutriments: edible food, contact as nutriment, volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment.
There are two types of feeling:
bodily feeling and mental feeling.
That which is associated with the five consciousnesses is called bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*);
that which is associated with the mental consciousness is called mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).
There are six [types] and three [kinds of] sensation.
These are the feeling of pain, the feeling of pleasure, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
There are seven feelings:

Eight-sixth, feelings:

There are one hundred and eight feelings,

Among these eighteen feelings:
There are those that are pure and those that are defiled;

Each of the three periods of time likewise possesses thirty-six.
There are one hundred and eight feelings.

superior, middling, and inferior.
There are three each for sorrow and equanimity;
thus, there are nine in one faculty.
Following the six faculties, there are fifty-four feelings.
Regarding the objects of present direct knowledge and inferential knowledge— namely, past and future feelings—
there are fifty-four feelings,

There are one hundred and eight types of feeling.
There are fifteen fruits: first, the sovereign fruit; second, the concordant fruit; third, the retributive fruit; fourth, the fruit of human effort; and fifth, the fruit of liberation.
It is called "fruit" because it is the recompense for causes.
The eleven [categories] are the six realms of existence:
namely, hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, devas, and asuras.
Twelve are the six elements:
namely, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
Thirteen are the seven stations of consciousness.
That is to say: the humans and devas of the desire realm constitute one;

There are fourteen [stations], including the eight abodes of merit (puṇyaprasava),

Fifteen are the eight worldly dharmas, namely:
gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and contempt, suffering and pleasure.

Seventeen abodes of sentient beings: that is,

Thus, in its very reality, it is without marks.
The "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya) is so named because it arises spontaneously and with mastery of intent.
In relation to future Buddhas, it is considered birth-and-death;
in relation to those who have not yet reached that stage, it is called a mind-made body because it is not yet fully perfected.

Question: Why is it that within the thicket of afflictions (*kleśa-gahana*), the teachings are divided into the two distinct categories of the initial and final [vehicles], whereas within the thickets of karma and birth (*karma-jāti-gahana*) there is no such division?
Answer: Afflictions are the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
For this reason, one must distinguish between the two types of karma-born [phenomena],
as these are their secondary characteristics.
The meaning can be understood by analogy with the preceding discussion on afflictions (*kleśa*).
Question: Since the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), why is it included within the "dense forest of birth" (*jāti-gahana*)?
Answer: The original intent for establishing the teaching on the death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) was to reveal that the Buddha-dharma is progressively profound and far-reaching;
thus, the death of transformation is placed after the death of segmented existence (*bhavāgra-cheda*).
This reveals that the Final Teaching (zhongjiao) is progressively more profound.
Judging by its underlying principle,
the生死 of transformation (bianyi shengsi) is merely the subtle aspect of the生死 of segmentation (fenduan).
This is how it is known:
the intermediate state (antarābhava) is fundamentally established as a segmented body;
it is established as the intermediate state because it serves as the means for seeking birth.
As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
this applies to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) and continues even unto nirvāṇa and bodhi.
There is also the intermediate state (antarābhava),
but it is subtle and increasingly profound;
it is the domain of the Buddhas alone.
Based on this scriptural evidence,
one should know that there is the death and rebirth of transformation (pariṇāmi-cyuti).
These are merely the subtle characteristics of the segmented [existence],
which undergo transformation as the twenty-five types of intermediate state bodies (antarābhava).
This is its retributive portion.
Its major period lasts for seven days as one limit,
though within that there is no fixed duration.
Whether for one day, two days, three days, four days,
or even for an entire kalpa,
the Buddha likewise appears in the world within that time to teach and transform beings.
They enter parinirvāṇa,
as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
and also as stated in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty.
For twenty years, the Buddha remained in the intermediate state (antarābhava);
this is also as stated in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
The intermediate state body (antarābhava) is likewise capable of performing karma and possesses its latent predispositions (vāsanā).
[This concludes] twenty-six [sections on] the three perceptions.
These refer to enemies, friends, and neutral persons.
The twenty-seven perceptions refer to the perception of impermanence regarding the permanent, up to the perception of purity regarding the impure.
Within this, its nature as grasping is distinguished.
Regarding the "perceptions of the twenty-eight [aspects of] the eight consciousnesses":
this means that the perceptions of the eight consciousnesses arise and perish simultaneously.
The meaning of the "dense forest of birth" explained above applies generally to the Śrāvakayāna as well as to humans, devas, and so forth.
If an ordinary person possesses the characteristics of a human being, [they are included therein].
If one were among those of the two vehicles,
there would be no separate person;
there would be only the real birth, the species, and the homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga), and so forth.
If one relies on the initial teaching,
the phase of arising is itself emptiness;
if one relies on the final teaching, [the phase of arising is not yet empty].
That which arises is itself suchness.
If it refers to the One Vehicle, it belongs to the One Vehicle; if it is discussed according to the Separate Teaching (prthagdeśanā), [it belongs to that].
This refers precisely to the eighty-four thousand marks of affliction (*kleśa*) and so forth;
it corresponds to the meanings of both *Indra* and "subtlety.
The remainder is as explained in other chapters.
Chapter on the Dense Forest of Habitual Tendencies: There are three kinds of habitual tendencies.
First, the habitual tendency of verbal expression and the habitual tendency of consciousness;
second, the habitual tendency of form-consciousness, the habitual tendency of object-consciousness, and the habitual tendency of view-consciousness.
The three types of perfuming— affliction-perfuming, karma-perfuming, and fruition-perfuming—
all these perfumings pertain to both the defiled and the pure, as well as the indeterminate.
There are two major types:
first, the perfuming of seeds;
second, the perfuming of the manifest mind.
This also applies to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*),
according to the superior, middling, and inferior grades, up to the immeasurable eighty-four thousand [dharmas] and so forth.
This is according to the Hīnayāna.
Its meaning is precisely reality;
the initial teaching is emptiness,
and the final teaching is suchness.
That which is designated as the One Vehicle is precisely the One Vehicle.
If considered according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), it is immeasurable.
The remainder is as in the separate chapter.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Dense Forest of the Practices of the Three Aggregates," there are five meanings to the term "dense forest" (*gahana*):
first, those who possess the nature for *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to those who have already departed from the spiritual lineage and lack the nature for nirvāṇa; that is,
those in the state of an icchantika.
Second, wholesome and unwholesome conduct;
third, the evil realms and the wholesome;
fourth, non-Buddhists and śrāvakas.
Fifth, the distinctions among bodhisattvas:
namely, the nominal bodhisattva (*prajñaptibodhisattva*),
as described in the text.
The eight wrong paths are:
wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
Because they arise without a proper direction, they are called "perverse" (邪).
As for the "Eightfold Right Path" (八正),
it is simply the reversal of the eight perverse paths, which constitutes the eight right [paths].
Regarding the dharmas such as the three aggregates,
if they belong to the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
their meaning is indeed real.
The initial teaching is the emptiness of phenomena;
the final teaching is suchness.
That which is designated by the One Vehicle is the entry into the One Vehicle.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on Attainment (*siddhi*):
"attainment" is also termed "acquisition" (*prāpti*).
This refers to the conventional designation of "acquisition" and "possession" with respect to wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, whether they increase or decrease.
The dharmas that are wholesome, unwholesome,
and indeterminate clarify the meaning of the basis;
as for their increase or decrease:
This reveals the meaning of its own nature. Why?
Because there is increase.
One is said to possess superior degrees of faith and so forth;
by virtue of their diminution,
one is said to possess inferior degrees of faith and so forth.
The phrase "provisionally established attainment" clarifies the meaning of "provisional establishment. When these three aspects— the meaning of establishment,
the meaning of attainment, and the meaning of possession— are present, it is called "attainment."
In this manner, one should understand that the establishment of the remaining cases is according to their respective requirements; furthermore,
there are three types of distinctions in the attainment of accomplishment.
That is to say: accomplishment of seeds,
accomplishment of mastery,
and accomplishment of manifestation.
Regarding the accomplishment of seeds:
this refers to the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm that arise when one is born in the desire realm.
It is accomplished by way of the accomplishment of seeds,
as well as the innate wholesome [states],
if one is born in the desire realm.
The afflictions and secondary afflictions of the three realms are possessed [by those] based on the description of ordinary worldlings who have not yet abandoned desire;
if one has already abandoned desire, [they are not].
Or, when born in a higher stage,
one is subject to the afflictions and secondary afflictions of that very stage corresponding to the level from which desire has been abandoned.
It is both accomplished and not accomplished;
for the latent tendencies (anuśaya) have not yet been permanently destroyed,
and it has been diminished by the path of antidote (pratipakṣa-mārga).
In their respective order,
as well as those wholesome states acquired at birth,
[they exist] according to the place where one is born.
This very stage is accomplished.
If one is born in the form realm,
the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the desire realm [are abandoned].
It is established by virtue of the accomplishment of seeds;
it is also termed non-accomplishment.
This refers to the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
It is accomplished by way of the accomplishment of seeds,
as well as innate wholesomeness;
this applies if one is born in the formless realm.
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the desire realm and the form realm are established by virtue of the possession of their seeds;
they are also termed "non-possession."
The afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the formless realm are accomplished by way of the accomplishment of their seeds,
as well as the innate wholesome [states].
If one has already attained the path that serves as the antidote to the three realms,
then according to each respective category,
the antidotes have accordingly arisen.
In this way and that way,
the seeds of various categories are either accomplished and attained, or not accomplished.
In accordance with this and that,
the various categories of remedies have not yet arisen;
in this and that manner [they shall arise].
A category is established by virtue of being established through its seeds.
One who has attained the path that serves as the antidote to the three realms refers to one who has already attained the supramundane noble path.
"According to such and such categories,
the antidotes have already arisen" means that the antidotes for the superior and other grades of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) have already arisen.
In this way,
regarding the attainment or non-attainment of the seeds of various types:
it refers to having already permanently destroyed the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Mastery and accomplishment refers to all skillful dharmas of expedient means,
as well as mundane and supramundane qualities such as dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti.
And a portion of indeterminate dharmas are accomplished by virtue of their mastery.
As for the wholesome dharmas of application:
This refers to the wisdom born of hearing and so forth;
although their seeds existed previously,
they would not manifest if separated from the present life.
Because, even when repeatedly practiced and increased,
they ultimately cannot arise as manifest;
such is one portion of indeterminate dharmas.
This refers to the mind of craftsmanship and the mind of transformation.
As for the accomplishment of manifest activity,
it refers to the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Whichever [state] is present—
whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—
one is "accomplished" therein by virtue of its manifestation.
If one has already severed the roots of goodness,
all wholesome dharmas are accomplished only through the accomplishment of their seeds.
It is also called non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
If one who is of the nature not to attain nirvāṇa (*aparinirvāṇadharman*) is ultimately possessed of the various defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*).
Because they lack the causes for liberation,
they are also called *ātyantika*;
this is because the causes for attaining liberation will never be accomplished.
Question: What is called the cause for attaining liberation?
Answer: If, regarding suchness, one has previously accumulated the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of afflictions, yet encounters favorable conditions that serve as antidotes.
One is then able to destroy it forever.
This state of being capable is called the cause for attaining liberation.
If one is contrary to this, [the opposite applies].
It is called "having no cause for liberation.
Question: What benefit is gained by being skillful in accomplishment?
Answer: One is able to thoroughly understand the increase and decrease of all phenomena.
Because they know increase and decrease,
they abandon the notion of certainty regarding the rise and fall of the world.
This method of accomplishment, which can even sever both craving and aversion,
pertains to the deluded śrāvakas.
This matter is not tenable;
if it were part of the initial teaching,
this principle would be inconsistent.
If it pertains to the Final Teaching (Jiǒngjiào),
because they are identical with Suchness (tathatā), it cannot be described.
Why is this? Because it is said that [such a view] merely increases conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*).
This is according to the separate teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*).
This is because it includes what was previously stated and excludes what was not;
other meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Twenty Kinds of Dharma Teachers," how is one able to perform the duties of a Dharma teacher?
First, the proper time;
second, right intention;
third, immediacy.
Fourth is continuity;
fifth is gradualness;
sixth is sequence.
Seventh is the gradual sequence of the meaning of the phrases;
eighth is indicating;
ninth is gladdening.
Tenth, exhortation;
eleventh, completeness;
twelfth, non-destruction.
Thirteenth, not being disorderly;
fourteenth, acting in accordance with the Dharma;
fifteenth, following the assembly.
Sixteenth is the mind of loving-kindness;
seventeenth is the mind of peace and security;
eighteenth is the mind of compassion.
Nineteenth, not being attached to gain, offerings, or fame.
Twentieth, not praising oneself or disparaging others.
Regarding the first [of these]:
One is free from the eight difficult times.
A verse in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) says:
"It is like a king who harbors anxiety, suffers from illness, is consumed by anger, is attached to various desires, or is in a perilous place."
When there are no attendants and no loyal ministers, but only sycophants and flatterers—
during these eight such times, a wise minister should not speak.
The King of the Mind is likewise.
One should not speak at an improper time.
The Dharma Master’s vocal karma is of two kinds;
thus, it is divided into two sections.
In the preceding section of the sutra, the Dharma Master expounds upon the profound and subtle meaning of the Dharma;
in the subsequent section, the Dharma Master explains the characteristics of eloquence in preaching the Dharma.
This meaning accords with the Three Vehicles.
The One Vehicle alone is ultimately definitive;
other meanings are as explained in separate chapters.
Regarding the Chapter on the Forty Unhindered Eloquences: as for "unhindered eloquence," it refers to...
This refers to the forty kinds of unimpeded eloquence.
Based upon ten dharmas,
and because each of these ten dharmas possesses four aspects, they constitute forty.
The reason ten are mentioned is to manifest their immeasurability,
as explained at length in the sutra.

Chapter Ten: The Receptivity-Consciousness of the Tenth Stage. Regarding the meaning of the receptivity-consciousness, it is briefly explained as being threefold: first, the receptivity-consciousness of objects; [second, the receptivity-consciousness of self-nature;
third, the receptivity-consciousness of the object’s characteristics]. (The second and third items are omitted here. First, the receptivity-consciousness of objects.
Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the consciousness of receiving [the teachings],
there are two principles for receiving consciousness,
as with those of the Three Vehicles.
The consciousness that realizes the jewel of principle is called the "consciousness of reception" (*vedanā-vijñāna*);
the third is the "consciousness of reception of both principle and phenomena," such as that of a Bodhisattva who has attained their rank.
Seated upon the great jewel lotus-king,
with the Buddhas of the ten directions emitting light to consecrate him and so forth,
that which internally corresponds to the dharma-realm is called the receiving consciousness (*vedanā-vijñāna*).
The details are as found in the dialogues and the scriptural texts.
Other meanings are treated in separate chapters.
Regarding the meaning of Lake Anavatapta, the *Anavatapta-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
The Anavatapta Lake flows forth as four rivers that course toward the great ocean;
Nirvāṇa further states:
There are eight rivers.
According to the Āgama and the Vibhāṣā,
there are twenty rivers.
The Lake Anavatapta has four animal mouths.
To the east is the golden elephant mouth,
from which the Ganges River flows forth.
To the west is the Silver Ox Mouth,
from which the Indus River flows;
to the south is the Lapis Lazuli Horse Mouth.
The Sītā River flows out from the northern Pāriyātra Lion’s Mouth;
the Vakṣu River flows out [from there as well].
Each of the four flows out for forty *li* and divides into five rivers, thus making twenty.
The Buddha was on the eastern side.
Most authorities who rely on renown state that there are eight rivers,
because they include the five rivers flowing toward the east along with the three great original rivers flowing toward the other three directions.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"From Lake Anavatapta flow four great rivers."
From each of the four mouths, [the rivers] emerge and circle the lake seven times;
thereafter, they exit toward the great ocean from their respective directions.
Such is the manner in which these rivers encircle it.
Each is separated from the next by one *li*.
Within them are various named flowers of diverse colors as adornments;
all these are the domains and boundaries of the Dragon King Anavatapta.
Now the Buddha cites the analogy of the ground for proof;
because the analogy is superior,
it reveals that the Dharma is likewise superior.
The remaining meanings may be understood.

The Chapter on the Ten Clarities (Daśavidyā-varga) within the Chapter on the Ten Clarities in the *Daśavidyā-parivarta*. Regarding the "Ten Clarities":
"Ten" is a number;
"clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to that which illuminates and penetrates its source, and is thus called "clarity."
This meaning applies throughout the ten stages;
it is precisely the virtue of the ten stages.
It is not shared with the three vehicles or the Hīnayāna.
The details are as extensively explained in the "Chapter on Transcending the World.
Regarding the chapter on the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there are three types of distinctions within the meditative attainment of cessation.
This refers to the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, and the Small Vehicle.
As for the meaning of the One Vehicle,
it means that the essence itself constitutes its function.
They transform and guide sentient beings and accomplish all the works of the Buddhas,
just as the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja entered the samādhi of cessation.
He immediately emits clouds of Dharma-realm bodies from his own person to benefit sentient beings.
As for those in the cessation samādhi of the three vehicles,
[he manifests] upon his own person.
It is not said that they accomplish their function by transforming themselves into different bodies and relying upon those distinct entities.
It accomplishes functions such as benefiting sentient beings;
thus it is termed "co-existent," with respect to the bodhisattva’s own person.
Thus, their characteristics cannot be described;
it is only by reference to the mental capacities of sentient beings that one can clarify the simultaneous practice of these bodhisattvas.
For those who practice the meditative concentrations of the Hīnayāna,
there is no aspect of benefiting others while remaining in equipoise; it is only after emerging from concentration that [such activity occurs].
It then constitutes a distinct entity.
As for its essence, the cessation-samādhi of the One Vehicle takes the dharma-realm as its essence;
furthermore, it arises from superior conditions.
To speak of this meaning of cessation is called "non-association.
Non-association is precisely the principle.
The definitive essence of the three vehicles is precisely the true nature of suchness (tathatā);
it is described as being non-correspondent (apratisaṃyukta) according to its superior conditions.
That which is non-associated is precisely the principle;
it is the principle of the One Vehicle.
The one is all; all is the one.
It encompasses both the Indra-like and the subtle, and so forth.
The principle of the Three Vehicles is simply a single quiescence; it does not speak of distinct characteristics,
and thus it is called "incompatible."
"Non-associated" means not being associated with conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
As for the "extinction-attainment" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the Hīnayāna:
It has non-association as its essence.
"Non-association" refers to the category of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
This refers to the clusters of dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Regarding the distinctions of stages (*avasthā-viśeṣa*),
this is according to the stages of the Hīnayāna.
Twelve people attain it;
that is, those who have extinguished the delusions regarding non-characteristics.
Eight people attain it.
Excluding those who are bound by all fetters,
this Mahāyāna is attained by the three types of practitioners at the initial stage of instruction: Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
This refers to those in the state of non-fixation, those in the state of fixation, and Buddhas.
Among these, the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;
it is as obtained by those in the state of non-fixation.
This is a concentration of the Hīnayāna,
because one has already attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) during the stage of the Hīnayāna.
Within the stage of direct progression in the Mahāyāna, four types of persons attain [the result]:
those in the indeterminate stage, those in the determinate stage, those in the eighth stage, and those in the Buddha stage.
The first two stages are identical to those of the Hīnayāna.
Because they first attained [the path] and later turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna],
if categorized according to the stages of the matured teachings (pakva-śāsana), five types of persons attain it;
in the indeterminate stage, there is one.
And there are two for the stage of fixed determination.
From the first bhūmi up to the sixth and seventh bhūmis, there are three;
from the eighth bhūmi upwards, there are four.
The fifth [category] is the Buddha-ground.
The first, the stage of non-fixed determination,
applies to both the initial teachings of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
Why is this? Because both individuals have turned their minds toward and entered the matured teaching (*pakva-śāsana*).
If one were to rely on the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*), it would be impossible to speak [of this].
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one attains [the fruit] across six stages:
from the initial stage of non-fixation and the stage of fixation, as well as the stage of liberation;
specifically, from the first thought-moment of the sixth stage, through the first bhūmi and above, up to the eighth bhūmi and above, and finally the Buddha-stage.
If one relies on the teachings of the *vipāka* (maturation),
regarding the turning of the mind from the Hīnayāna,
it is based on the virtues of the distinct ten stages (*bhūmi*).
It is attained in the sixth bhūmi; however,
if one considers those who directly advance according to the initial teaching or those who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna],
it is attained in the same manner as in the seventh bhūmi.
If those of the Mature Teaching and others turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna],
they attain it based on the characteristics of the ten distinct stages of the Perfect Teaching;
it is attained at the eighth stage.
One attains that extinction concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Why is this?
Because the extinction concentrations of the Three Vehicles [are distinct].
Because these have already been attained previously.
The remaining meanings are as explained in other chapters.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences" within the "Section on the Ten Patiences": the ten patiences are as follows.

Namely: the patience that accords with sounds, the patience of compliance, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena, the patience like an illusion, the patience like a mirage, the patience like a dream, the patience like an echo, the patience like lightning, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space.
This patience (kṣānti) pervades all ten stages (bhūmi).
The reason for speaking of ten is to manifest its immeasurability.
A detailed explanation is provided in a separate chapter.
Regarding the "Chapter on Incalculable Time-Ages" within the "Chapter on Incalculables":
as for what constitutes an incalculable period (*asaṃkhyeya-kāla*), there are differences between the Mahāyāna and the two vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha.
In the Hīnayāna, sixty kalpas constitute a great kalpa-asaṃkhyeya;
according to the Hīnayāna sūtras, one attains Buddhahood after passing through these three asaṃkhyeyas.
The Mahāyāna meanings from the *Kulika* [chapter] onwards constitute one hundred phrases,
which is termed "one reception" (*ekodgraha*).
From "one reception" onwards...
It is called one *asaṃkhyeya*.
This is a great number;
it is the first number among the ten numerical categories.
The Buddhas of the Three Vehicles and the Mahāyāna employ only a single method of transformation;
they pass through these three great kalpas.
One attains Buddhahood through the cultivation of the path.
If according to the meaning of the Sudden Teaching, it cannot be described;
if according to the meaning of the One Vehicle, it spans inexhaustible eons.
Why is this? Because, based on the One Vehicle, all sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood,
and yet for the sake of sentient beings, they continue to attain Buddhahood anew and ever anew.
Nor does one attain perfect enlightenment while remaining on the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*).
Since this is not limited by time, it is inexhaustible.
This is the teaching regarding this meaning.
One generates faith by comparing and weighing the virtues of the ten stages.
Furthermore, as for these numerical dharmas:
This [attainment] is acquired through the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Other meanings are as explained in the separate chapter.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Distinctions of Lifespan" within the "Chapter on Lifespan": as for "lifespan," [The text continues: ...lifespan refers to the duration of life. It is of two kinds: first, the lifespan of the physical body; second, the lifespan of the mental continuum. The lifespan of the physical body is determined by the maturation of karma and the conditions of the four great elements. The lifespan of the mental continuum is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the force of vows. as well as the meaning of the temporal limits of the causes of the worlds.
In the second assembly, the oceans of pure lands and the methods for accomplishing the stages of faith, understanding, and practice were taught.
In the third assembly, the Dharma of the Ten Abodes was taught,
as well as the clarification of the Dharmas of Dharmas.
In the fourth assembly, the Dharma of the Ten Practices and the Dharma of the Ten Treasuries were taught.
In the fifth assembly, the Dharma of the Ten Dedications was taught.
In the sixth assembly, the causes, effects, virtues, and functions of the Ten Stages, as well as the teachings on Samantabhadra’s Nature-Arising and so forth, were taught.
In the seventh re-assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall, the Dharma of Transcending the World was taught.
The eighth assembly explains the Dharma of entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
According to the Sanskrit manuscript from the Great Ci'en Monastery, a ninth assembly is added,
concerning the Buddha’s journey to the foot of a tree and the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka*).

Question: For what reason have all that has been recorded above been distinct and different?
Answer: It refers to the characteristics of the doctrinal gateways revealed in the fundamental text of the Great Sūtra;
that is, the teachings and meanings in which principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated and sovereign, wherein the one is all.
All is one. Like the analogy of Indra’s net, they are inexhaustible and not identical,
as is the case with the nets of various teachings.
The primary and its attendants manifest one another;
to claim they possess fixed characteristics would contradict the Great Principle.
The distinctions between the primary and the attendant aspects of the sūtras differ,
as explained in the *Bhūmi-sūtra* regarding the six definitive meanings.
This is the essential substance of these stages;
conversely, they are not designated by the number ten.
The ten stages are not identical.
This is the characteristic of that ground.
It is designated by reversing the use of the number ten;
through this, one may verify and come to know it.
Out of his great compassion, the Buddha, wishing to make it easy to understand,
took the substance of a number that was incomplete and expressed it through the characteristic of a complete number.
This is the Buddha’s specific intention.
Now, according to the *Yingluo benye jing* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*,
these numbers are reconciled to be complete as ten.
The original versions of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra contain only seven or eight [chapters] and are incomplete;
their meanings should be understood accordingly.
As for the two sūtras, the *Yingluo benye jing* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
These two vehicles are subsumed [within the three-vehicle teaching],
whereas the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is subsumed within the One Vehicle. Why is this?
The meaning of the number ten contains two gates:
first, the gate of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya).
Second, the gate of the incomplete Perfect Teaching.
Now, I shall contrast the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts with the original version of the Great Sūtra.
The ten categories, such as the *ratna-avalī* (necklace) and so forth,
are "single and distinct," because they do not possess the entirety of the perfect [teachings].
They are included within the three vehicles and do not fully possess the ten numerical categories;
furthermore, they are of two kinds.
The first clarifies the three vehicles for people to analyze and understand;
the second clarifies the one vehicle.
Regarding those of inferior capacity,
the One Vehicle is revealed through contrast;
now, this is based on the gate of revelation through contrast.
Those teachings that do not fill the ten numbers are subsumed within the One Vehicle;
the rest may be understood by analogy.

The Meaning of the Delimitation of the Teachings Used to Authenticate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Now, based on the sevenfold teachings, I shall authenticate the textual and doctrinal delimitations of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
First, the sūtras:

namely, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Āgama of the Original Vows of the Garland*, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata), and so forth.
Second, the śāstras.
These refer to the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, the *Tattvārtha-śāstra*, and so forth;
as well as the three commentaries and the four topical outlines.

On the Differences and Similarities of the Sanskrit Texts: Based on the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from the Great Ci'en Monastery, it was examined that there are five hundred and forty-one folios, with fifty-five characters per line.
Twenty lines constitute one folio.
On the reverse side of one folio, there are two thousand two hundred and eighty characters.
Ten folios amount to twenty-two thousand eight hundred characters.
Thirty-two characters constitute one verse (*śloka*).
One hundred sheets amount to two hundred and twenty-eight thousand characters.
Three hundred and twenty thousand [characters] constitute ten thousand verses.
It consists of five hundred and forty-one folios,
totaling one million three hundred twenty-three thousand four hundred eighty characters. According to the standard of thirty-two characters per verse,
this constitutes [forty-two thousand nine hundred thirty-seven] verses.
The total count is approximately forty-one thousand nine hundred and eighty stanzas, plus ten characters.

This teaching explains that the cultivation [of the path] achieves greatness,
because it is taught that Buddhahood is realized while still within the causal stage.
This has two meanings.

now, this shall be explained according to the teachings.
First, the teaching on the accomplishment of cultivation through names;

The teaching on names explains that cultivation achieves greatness;
this teaching on cultivation applies throughout two great stages: the stage of causal achievement and the stage of gradual causal achievement.
